item.title: CamusDB in production at Bacon Games: a first-party report
item.description: What Bacon Games runs on CamusDB since 2025, how teams use database branches, what failed, and what this report does not prove.
item.content:encoded:
This post describes the CamusDB deployment at Bacon Games: the workload, the cluster, how teams use database branches, the defects that our backend found in CamusDB, and the data that stays on other systems. If you are evaluating CamusDB, it shows you one real production system and its limits.

I wrote CamusDB, and I am the CTO of Bacon Games. This is a report from the team that builds the database, about its own production use. It is evidence that CamusDB runs a real workload. It is no endorsement from an independent customer, and no independent production user is public yet.

What runs on CamusDB​

Bacon Games has used CamusDB since 2025. It is the backend database for many games. All games use one backend platform, and each system of that platform stores its data in CamusDB:

Kind of dataSystems
Player valueWallets and currencies, inventories and item upgrades, rewards, code redemption
PurchasesThe store, in-app purchase receipts, checkout orders, the transaction log
PlayersUsers, identity, devices, sessions, consent records, player statistics
SocialSocial features, presence, leaderboards
Live operationsGame configs, parameters, game events, feature flags, experiments, player segments, scheduled jobs
Messages and contentThe player inbox, player mail, news, localization
MarketingInstall attribution, ad placements, ad conversions

The first group is a ledger. A wallet must never go below zero, an item has exactly one owner, and a reward is granted once. We explained why that workload needs serializable transactions, with a trade between two players in SQL, in Game wallets and inventories need distributed transactions.

The other groups are ordinary relational data. They live in the same database as the ledger, so a purchase, the inventory change, and the inbox message that confirms it can commit in one transaction.

Branches in daily work​

A database branch is an isolated copy of a database that shares the data of its source. A write to the branch never reaches the source. Two teams use branches every day.

Customer support and QA create a branch to examine the case of one player. They can repeat a purchase, grant an item, or run a fix against the real state of that player, and the live data does not change.

Developers create a branch of the development database and work there. A schema change or a test data set of one developer does not break the work of another developer. When the work is done, the developer drops the branch.

The statement is the same in both cases. The names here are examples:

CREATE DATABASE support_case_4812 BRANCH FROM game_prod;

The deployment​

Used since2025
CamusDB version today0.18
ModeCluster mode
Nodes3, each with 4 cores and 16 GB of memory
Where it runsGoogle Cloud
Replication factor3
ClientThe EF Core provider, over gRPC
BackupsPoint-in-time recovery

With three nodes and a replication factor of 3, every node holds a copy of every partition. A write commits when two of the three copies accept it, so the cluster keeps committing while one node is down.

Point-in-time recovery restores the database to a chosen moment inside a retention window, in addition to the moment of the last backup.

Why we run our own database​

Before CamusDB, our games used MongoDB, DynamoDB and Google Cloud Spanner.

MongoDB/DynamoDB. Our data had no enforced structure, so all validation logic lived in the application. Queries that needed joins were hard to write without SQL. The transaction support was too limited for our ledger data.

Google Spanner. It gave us SQL and strong transactions across servers, and it showed us that a database can provide consistency and scale together. It was also costly for our workload, and it was a closed system for us: we could not read the engine, and we could not extend it. It had no database branches, no query result cache, and none of the other features that we later built into CamusDB, such as C# extensions.

CockroachDB/YugabyteDB. These are distributed SQL databases with available source code, and we considered them. Two things kept us from them. A different company directs each product and decides its roadmap and its license. They are also built on other technology: CockroachDB is written in Go, and YugabyteDB is written in C and C++.

That second point matters to us because Bacon Games is a .NET studio. All of our developers work in C#. With CamusDB, the game, the backend, and the database use one language and one toolchain. A backend developer can read the database source, debug it with the usual tools, and write a trigger or a function in C# that runs inside the server.

These are the reasons of one team with one workload. All four products are mature, and all of them run systems much larger than ours.

We chose CamusDB because we build it, so our judgment of this choice has a bias. A team that does not build CamusDB must compare it with PostgreSQL and with the established distributed SQL databases for its own workload. Why CamusDB? lists the cases where CamusDB is a weaker fit, and The origins of CamusDB gives the longer history.

Defects that our backend found​

Our backend is the first heavy user of each CamusDB release, so it finds defects before other users do. We keep a record of each one. This is that record.

Two defects had the largest effect:

A commit that never returned. EF Core saved the changes inside an explicit transaction, and the commit that followed did not complete and gave no error. Config writes from our operations portal stopped. A driver release fixed it.

A filter that became slower with each row. A filter with a correlated EXISTS subquery ran the subquery as a scan for each candidate row, at 3 to 30 ms per row. A filtered page of an inventory with 300 items reached the 10-second timeout. The query also became slower when other players had more rows. The planner now reads the subquery table through its primary key, the same queries on 1,200 items complete promptly, and two regression tests hold that result.

The full list:

AreaDefectStatus
TransactionsThe commit did not return after EF Core saved changes in an explicit transactionFixed
TransactionsThe driver rejected the Read Committed isolation levelFixed. We use it for append-only writes such as receipts and the transaction log
TransactionsA bulk insert in a read-only transaction preset reported success, and no row was storedThe preset is read-only by design. We use a read-write preset
SchemaA unique index on a nullable column rejected a second NULLFixed
SchemaThe migration history check always answered "no migrations", so each migration looked pendingFixed
SchemaTwo concurrent CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS statements for one name: one can fail with "already registered"Open in the server. The driver accepts the error as success
Query translationEF Core AnyAsync was not supportedFixed
Query translationA negated boolean column, !row.IsDeleted, was a syntax errorFixed
Query translationStartsWith with a StringComparison argument was not translatedFixed
Query translationlist.Contains(column) threw an exception before the query ranFixed
Query translationA negated correlated EXISTS was rejectedFixed
ResultsA UUID column that passed through a join had the wrong type, and the row could not be readFixed in the server and in the driver
ResultsThe driver looked up a column by name with exact case, while SQL ignores caseFixed
PerformanceA correlated EXISTS filter ran as a scan for each rowFixed
JSONBA driver older than 0.17 reads a JSONB cell as NULL over gRPC, with no errorOpen. Upgrade each client before you add a JSONB column

Twelve of the fifteen entries are fixed. The entries that remain are one server defect with a driver workaround, one preset that needs a clear error, and one upgrade order that you must follow.

Most of these defects are in the driver, the EF Core provider, and the query planner. Caraxes, our fault-injection harness, tests a different layer: it kills nodes, cuts the network, and fills disks while it checks that no committed data is lost. A real application that uses the provider every day found what the fault tests do not look for.

What does not run on CamusDB​

Analytics data runs in ClickHouse. ClickHouse is an analytics database, and CamusDB is built for transactions. Large scans and aggregations over event history belong in a system that is designed for them.

What this report shows​

  • CamusDB holds authoritative production data for a real product.
  • It replaced MongoDB and Spanner for many games, and it has run in production since 2025.
  • Database branches are part of the daily work of support, QA, and development.

It does not show these things:

  • That CamusDB fits a workload that is different from ours.
  • How CamusDB behaves at a size larger than the deployment above.
  • That a team without the authors of the database can operate it. We fix the engine ourselves when production finds a defect.

CamusDB is still young, and APIs and storage formats can change between versions. See Current scope.

If you want to try CamusDB and find anything to improve tell us in a GitHub issue. A report from an independent team is worth more to other readers than this one.

item.title: CamusDB and CockroachDB on the same host: a serializable bank benchmark
item.description: A contended bank workload with serializable transactions on three-node CamusDB and CockroachDB clusters, why the old CamusDB default was slower, and the three changes that replaced its row lock.
item.content:encoded:
This post compares serializable transactions on three-node CamusDB and CockroachDB clusters, on one bank workload where transactions often collide. You will see where the old CamusDB default was slower, which row lock caused it, and the three changes that replaced the lock. If you are evaluating CamusDB for transactional workloads, the tables and the open issues show what to expect today.

In a distributed database, writes and strongly consistent reads require coordination across multiple nodes, which limits throughput. Every write must be synchronously replicated to other nodes, wait for a majority to persist and acknowledge it, and only then return a confirmation to the client.

Reads face similar challenges. The system needs to verify that the node serving the results is still the leader to avoid inconsistencies. On top of that, network latency, buffers, and queues can all become bottlenecks as the workload increases.

These challenges aren't unique to CamusDB. Other strongly consistent distributed databases, such as Spanner and CockroachDB, have had to solve similar problems. Traditional single-node databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL don't face these same challenges. They make different architectural tradeoffs, favoring single-node performance over some of the guarantees and capabilities of distributed systems.

Throughout CamusDB's development, the goal has been to improve performance without weakening strong consistency.

To understand how CamusDB performs against established databases, I decided to benchmark it against CockroachDB (a distributed SQL database written in Go). This felt like a more apples-to-apples comparison. Comparing it with PostgreSQL or MySQL wouldn't be entirely fair, since they're designed to solve similar problems but take fundamentally different architectural approaches.

Results in brief​

Both databases ran on one 16-core laptop, three nodes each, at the Serializable isolation level. Serializable is the strictest level: the result is the same as if the transactions ran one at a time.

  • CockroachDB v26.3.5 completed 7,389 operations per second.
  • CamusDB with its single-row read locks, the default when the comparison began, completed 6,857, and gave up on 0.3% of transfers.
  • CamusDB without those locks, the default now, completed 12,618, with no failed transfer.

CamusDB locked every row it read, although its storage layer already validates those reads at commit. It took three changes to replace the lock. The lock-free form is now the CamusDB default, and a setting restores the locks. The default changed on the day of the last measurement, and it is not in a release yet. The changes for applications and the open issues are below.

Before it became the default, the lock-free form passed three full runs of our nightly consistency checks and three 2-hour fault soaks.

Read CockroachDB's numbers with care. Running three nodes on the same machine is probably far from ideal. Its settings might not be properly tuned for maximum performance (probably ignorance on my end), or its defaults might be optimized for different types of workloads. This post focuses on CamusDB with the row locks and on the lock-free form.

This is one workload on one host. The limits are listed below.

Workload and setup​

The workload is the bank test from the 10K ops/sec post: a table of 2,000 accounts. Half of the operations are single-row balance reads. The other half are transfers between two accounts:

BEGIN;

SELECT balance, version FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @low_id;
UPDATE workload_accounts
SET balance = @low_balance, version = version + 1 WHERE id = @low_id;

SELECT balance, version FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @high_id;
UPDATE workload_accounts
SET balance = @high_balance, version = version + 1 WHERE id = @high_id;

COMMIT;

256 concurrent workers on 2,000 rows make transfers collide often. When the database rejects a transfer because of a conflict, the client retries it, up to ten attempts.

After each run, a reconciliation checks that the sum of balances is unchanged and that each row's version matches the committed transfers.

The host is a laptop with an Intel Core i7-13620H (16 logical cores) and 31 GiB of memory. It runs the three nodes and the load generator. Each node keeps a full copy of the table (replication factor 3), and one node, the leader, orders the writes. Each node's container is limited to 8,192 MiB, with data on a 6,144 MiB memory-backed file system (tmpfs). Each run has a 6-minute warm-up and a 10-minute measured window.

CamusDBCockroachDB
VersionDevelopment build on Kahuna.Core 1.16.7 to 1.16.9, .NET 10v26.3.5
IsolationSerializable, optimistic lockingSerializable (default)
Layout1 partition, one leader16 ranges after load splitting, leases spread over 3 nodes
ClientCamusDB .NET client 0.18.1, 256 workers over 64 logical connectionsNpgsql 9.0.4, 256 connections
Memory settingsDefaults for the limit--cache=.25 --max-sql-memory=.25

Some terms in the table:

  • Optimistic locking: a transaction works without waiting for other transactions. The database checks for conflicts and rejects the loser.
  • Partition and range: a slice of a table with its own leader. CamusDB calls it a partition and CockroachDB calls it a range.
  • Load splitting: CockroachDB divides a busy range into smaller ranges, and different nodes can lead them.

Results​

CamusDB, with read locks (the old default)CamusDB, without them (the new default)CockroachDB
Operations per second6,85712,6187,389
Retries per transfer0.4120.1100.079
Transfers that gave up after 10 attempts6,203 (0.3%)00
Read p50 / p95 / p99 (ms)0.75 / 5.3 / 14.01.7 / 7.4 / 18.47.2 / 38.2 / 62.2
Transfer p50 / p95 / p99 (ms)58.1 / 136.2 / 241.932.1 / 65.5 / 97.349.0 / 135.0 / 216.7
Cluster CPU per operation (ms)1.380.871.98
Peak memory per node (GiB)4.5 to 4.76.93.4 to 3.8
ReconciliationPassPassPass

p50, p95, and p99 are the latencies that 50%, 95%, and 99% of operations stayed under.

A second run of CamusDB with the locks gave 6,828 operations per second. CockroachDB with load splitting disabled reached 8,132.

  • CockroachDB was CPU-bound on this host. Its nodes used 14.6 of the 16 cores, and the load generator used the same machine.
  • CamusDB uses more memory. In the faster configuration, its nodes peak near twice CockroachDB's figure.
  • CockroachDB retries less. It retried one transfer in thirteen. The faster CamusDB configuration retried one in nine.

Row locks slowed the old default​

Under Serializable, CamusDB took a shared lock on every row that a read-write transaction read. Many transactions can hold a shared lock on one row. To write the row, a transaction must upgrade to an exclusive lock, which only one transaction can hold. CamusDB took these locks with optimistic locking too. On this workload they had three costs.

A slower commit. A transaction on one partition can commit in one phase. A transaction that holds a row lock must use the two-phase commit, which adds a prepare round. 3,317,003 of 3,317,020 commits took the two-phase path, at 26.0 ms on the server against 13.8 ms.

Upgrade conflicts. Two transfers that read the same row both hold a shared lock, and neither can upgrade while the other holds it. The younger one aborts. A retried transfer is always the youngest, so it tends to lose again. 6,203 transfers lost ten times in a row.

Polling. A transaction that waits for a lock sleeps 1, 2, 4, and up to 50 ms, and asks again. One run recorded 3.0 million sleeps.

Three changes that replaced the lock​

Kahuna, the key/value storage layer under CamusDB, records every read of an optimistic transaction with the row revision it saw, or the fact that the key was missing. At commit, it rejects the transaction if any of those reads is out of date. A key that is read and then written goes through the same check.

So the lock on a single row adds nothing to what gets committed. But the lock also did two other jobs, and each one needed its own replacement.

1. Reads are validated at commit​

A read of a single row takes no lock. The setting serializable_optimistic_point_locks: true restores the lock.

Scans keep their range locks. A row inserted into a scanned range is a new key, and a check of the keys the scan saw cannot find it.

2. A read floor keeps the rows of one transaction consistent​

Without the lock, a transaction could read two rows from two different moments. For example, two accounts hold 100 each:

The database refused the reader's commit, but the application had the two values first.

Each transaction now has a floor: a moment at which every row it read still held the value it read. A read of a new row has two paths:

  • If the row is unchanged since the floor, the read is served at once. On the bank workload, 82% of second-row reads take this path.
  • If the row changed, the database checks the earlier rows again. It refuses the read if one of them changed.

The floor costs about 3% of throughput.

3. A younger writer gives way to an older reader​

With locks, the younger of two conflicting transactions is refused at its first statement, and the older one proceeds.

Without locks, a younger transaction could stage its write. The older transaction that had read the row was then refused at commit, after it did all its work. On workloads with a few very hot keys, that cost a third to a half of the committed transactions.

A write or a delete now gives way at once to an older transaction that read the row and is still running. That restores the order the lock gave.

Results on workloads with hot keys​

The bank workload picks rows uniformly. To test a few constantly contended keys, we used the workloads of Elle. Elle is the checker of the Jepsen project: it reads a history of operations and searches for consistency anomalies. Its workloads pick keys from a skewed distribution.

  • List-append: transactions append to lists and read them.
  • Read-write register: transactions read and write single values.
  • Predicate reads: transactions read rows that match a condition.
  • Explicit, pipelined, and autocommit: three ways in which a client sends a transaction.

The table shows committed transactions in 60 seconds at Serializable with optimistic locking, on the same host, in back-to-back runs.

WorkloadLocks onWithout the locks, before change 3Without the locks, all three changes
List-append, explicit, 1 node56,06036,79466,620
List-append, pipelined, 1 node56,492Not measured64,283
List-append, autocommit, 1 node140,826Not measured189,796
Read-write register, explicit, 1 node35,831Not measured35,122
Read-write register, pipelined, 1 node36,296Not measured35,853
Read-write register, autocommit, 1 node83,428Not measured81,820
List-append, explicit, 3 nodes41,358Not measured46,765
Read-write register, explicit, 3 nodes27,626Not measured25,988
Predicate reads, explicit, 1 node13,606Not measured14,529
Predicate reads, pipelined, 1 node13,491Not measured13,665
Predicate reads, autocommit, 1 node135,497Not measured135,042
Predicate reads, explicit, 3 nodes10,962Not measured10,675

With all three changes, the lock-free form is 13% to 35% ahead of the locks on list-append. It is level on read-write register and on predicate reads. The read-write register cell on three nodes is 6% behind, and one run of each cannot separate that from noise.

Elle judged every history in this table serializable.

Tests of the lock-free form​

Elle. The nightly matrix runs list-append, read-write register, and predicate-read histories on one node and on three, at every isolation level, locking mode, and wire mode. A cell fails on any anomaly that its isolation level forbids. With the lock-free form as the default, the matrix passed in full three times: with the first two changes, then with all three, then with deletes included. A second nightly job of 18 fault and placement scenarios also passed all three times.

Anomaly tests. Ten interleavings in which a commit of both transactions breaks serializability, each run with the locks on and off:

  • Write skew: two transactions read the same rows, and each writes a different row based on what it read.
  • A lost update: two transactions read a row, and both write it.
  • A decision on a row that another transaction then changed.
  • A decision on a missing row that another transaction then inserted.
  • A phantom: a row that another transaction inserts into a scanned table.
  • A row read through a join.
  • Rows read by an IN list.
  • Rows that an inverted-index read examined and dropped.
  • A large value.
  • A row that one transaction read and a younger transaction deleted.

At most one transaction commits in each. One more test checks that a reader never receives the 100-and-150 mix.

Fault soaks. A fault soak is a long run in which the test harness injects failures. Three soaks ran 2 hours each on durable storage with 14 faults: six leader kills (two of them for 2 and 4 minutes), pauses, and slow-disk windows. One soak ran after each change.

Change 1 onlyChanges 1 and 2All three changes
VerdictPassPassPass
ReconciliationExactExactExact
Operations per second5,1485,0414,925
Leader failover after a kill3 to 4 s2 to 4 s1 to 3 s
Nodes that died on their own000
Peak memory per node2.4 to 2.6 GiB of 4 GiB2.4 to 2.6 GiB of 4 GiB2.4 to 2.6 GiB of 4 GiB
Transfers that ran out of attempts293 of 19 million399 of 18 million416 of 18 million

The three soaks ran on different days on a drive whose speed varies, so the throughput figures are not a trend. The transfers that ran out of attempts come from the read wait described below.

The full test suite. We ran it with the new default before the commit. It found one defect: the lock-free form also changed Read Committed transactions, and refused younger writers that the old form accepted. The lock-free form now applies to Serializable transactions only.

Changes for applications and open issues​

  • A conflict is reported at a different moment. A reader no longer blocks a writer. A conflict that the lock refused at the writer's statement can now be refused at the reader's next read, or at the reader's commit. After each refusal, the application can retry the transaction from the start.
  • Readers on another node. A write gives way only to an older reader whose session runs on the node that leads the row. We tried to count readers on other nodes, and it showed no gain on three nodes.
  • Transfers run out of attempts during a stall. See the read wait below. 33 of the 399 in the second soak were a read that kept answering "retry". The third soak had none, so they look tied to the moments of that run's faults. They are not traced.
  • Reconciliation proves less than serializability. It proves balances and versions for the bank workload. Elle is the serializability evidence.
  • Memory. The lock-free runs peak at 6.9 GiB of an 8 GiB limit in ten minutes.

Client streams, read waits, and Read Committed​

More client streams​

The CamusDB client sent all 64 logical connections over two network streams. A raise of the default to eight streams (client 0.18.1) cut read p50 from 2.87 ms to 1.71 ms.

Reads wait for an uncommitted write​

A writer that lost a race used to poll the winner's uncommitted row. With Kahuna.Core 1.16.7, a read waits behind the uncommitted write and wakes when that write commits or aborts.

The setting optimistic_intent_wait_ms (default 100) limits the wait. Measured at Read Committed, retries per transfer fell from 0.362 to 0.108.

The wait has one known cost. A retry now takes about 105 ms, so ten attempts are spent in about a second. When a server stalls for longer, the transfers queued behind the stalled writer give up: about 300 of 19 million in each fault soak, against 12 before. The remedy is not chosen.

Two changes that did not help​

  • A pause of the client after its write gave way removed wasted attempts, but committed 4% to 21% fewer transactions. A refused attempt is cheap, and an immediate retry gets in sooner.
  • A count of readers on other nodes changed nothing measurable.

Read Committed results​

Read Committed is a weaker isolation level that permits anomalies which Serializable forbids. On the bank workload, CamusDB at Read Committed with optimistic locking completes 12,870 operations per second. CockroachDB at Read Committed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE completes 5,412. The two configurations do different things, so the Serializable results are the comparison.

Limits of the comparison​

  • The default is new. The lock-free form became the default on the day of the last measurement. It is not in a release yet.
  • One host. Nodes and the load generator share 16 cores, which penalizes the system that uses more CPU. The 10-minute runs have no network latency and no durable disk.
  • One workload, small data. 2,000 hot rows on one partition favor a single-leader layout. CockroachDB is built to spread ranges over many nodes, and this test gives it little to spread.
  • Different clients. Npgsql with 256 connections, against a client that shares a few network streams.
  • Defaults, lightly tuned. CockroachDB ran at defaults apart from the memory flags. An expert could likely tune both databases further.
  • Single runs. Same-build noise on the bank workload is about 0.5% for CamusDB. The CockroachDB run was not repeated. The 60-second Elle cells vary by a few percent between runs.

Planned work on the setting and the comparison​

  • Choose the remedy for transfers that run out of attempts during a stall.
  • Repeat the comparison on separate machines with durable disks.

item.title: How much we test CamusDB
item.description: About 5.4 million operations per night, 23 to 39 million in each daily two-hour fault soak, what each harness checks, how often the nightly jobs fail, and what the numbers do not prove.
item.content:encoded:
This post shows how much testing stands behind CamusDB: about 5.4 million operations per night, 23 to 39 million operations in each daily two-hour fault soak, and more than 21,000 automated tests. You will see where these numbers come from and what they do not prove.

Test volume per night​

SourceWhat runsVolume per nightBasis
Caraxes nightly94 scenarios, most with Elle history checks5.1M operationsCounted on November 6
SQL fuzzer5 oracles, 60 seconds each172,112 statementsCounted on November 6
Kahuna Jepsen26 jobs100,167 operationsCounted on November 6
Kommander Jepsen13 jobsAbout 20,000 operationsCounted in 6 jobs, estimated for the rest
Total per nightAbout 5.4M

These counts describe the current schedule. The nightly Elle matrix started on November 3 and the scheduled SQL fuzzer started on November 4, so you cannot multiply these numbers by the age of the project.

The fault soak: volume​

A soak is a long run that shows what a short run cannot: memory that creeps, logs that grow, and recovery that gets slower. Caraxes, our database test tool, runs a bank soak for two hours every day, and we also use it to accept new versions of the storage stack.

The bank workload moves money between accounts in a table of 2,000 rows, so transactions collide on purpose. After the run, the total balance must be exactly the same as at the start.

The workload has two kinds of operation, in equal parts:

  • A read reads one row by its primary key.
  • A transfer reads two rows, updates two rows and commits. The whole transaction counts as one operation.

Our throughput post recorded fault soaks at 3,230 to 5,485 operations per second. Over two hours, that is 23 to 39 million operations, and about 12 to 20 million of them are transfers. These rates are approximate and depend on the host. The figures are calculated from those rates and are not a count from one run.

The same post measured 10,284 operations per second with no faults, for 45 minutes self-hosted storage. That is a separate run and is not part of the soak figures.

The fault soak kills the leader, freezes processes and throttles a disk, with 14 faults in the window. Part three of the dragon series lists the pass rules: exact balances, no unresolved commit, no lost or duplicated row, and no two replicas that apply one log entry differently.

The daily soak runs on a dedicated Linux machine at our company, not on GitHub Actions. The reason is capacity: a two-hour soak needs steady CPU and disk for three nodes and a load generator, and the shared GitHub runners cannot give that. The soak scenarios are public, so you can run the same soak on your own hardware. The fixes are public too, as the commits below show.

The nightly jobs: depth​

The soak gives volume, but a total balance check cannot see every kind of anomaly. So the nightly jobs check less data more closely.

JobWhat it checksLast count (November 6)
Caraxes Elle matrix3 transaction shapes, 1 and 3 nodes, each isolation level, locking mode and wire mode76 scenarios, 4.7M operations
Caraxes append and bank scenariosNo faults, partitions, kills, clock jumps, leader transfers, range splits, replica moves18 scenarios, 348,000 operations
SQL fuzzerThe same query must give the same answer under every plan1,672 rounds, 172,112 statements, 56,622 checks
Kahuna JepsenThe transactional storage layer under CamusDB, with faults26 jobs, 100,167 operations
Kommander JepsenThe Raft consensus layer under Kahuna, with faults13 jobs, about 20,000 operations
Kommander random searchGenerated fault plans on real three-node clusters38 seeds, 352 tests passed, 38 skipped
Plan qualityQuery plans on two benchmark query sets, one of them the Join Order Benchmark212 queries

Elle reads the full history of a run and looks for isolation anomalies such as lost updates and write skew. Before any Elle scenario runs, the job gives Elle histories with known verdicts. A checker that passes a lost update would make every green result meaningless.

Jepsen is a widely used tool that tests distributed systems under faults. The Jepsen counts are small on purpose. The clients run at 10 requests per second each, because the cost of the check grows quickly with the size of the history, and a checker can fully judge a short history. These two harnesses test the layers under CamusDB, not its SQL.

A weekly job adds a long arm: 12 Elle scenarios, each of which must reach one million committed transactions or fail. Its first scheduled run is on November 8, so the totals above do not include it.

The test suites​

Each push to a main branch runs the full test suite of that repository. The last run of each suite on November 6 had these totals:

RepositoryTests
CamusDB (including plan quality)11,843
Kahuna5,443
Kommander3,457
Caraxes456
Total21,199

Failure rate of the nightly jobs​

A volume number without its failures tells you little. These are the scheduled runs to date:

JobSinceRunsPassedFailed or cancelled
Kahuna JepsenAugust 5945737
Kommander JepsenAugust 13867610
Kommander random searchSeptember 4644816
Caraxes append and bank scenariosSeptember 25433310
Plan qualityOctober 1523221
Caraxes Elle matrixNovember 3431
SQL fuzzerNovember 4330

A failed night means "download the results and look". It is not always a database defect, because these jobs run on shared CI machines and a slow machine can also fail a run. We did not classify each failure for this post. The defects that these jobs and Caraxes did find are in the dragon series.

Three defects the soak found this week​

On November 4 and 5, three soaks in a row each found a new problem. These runs added kills of 2 and 4 minutes to the fault schedule. After a long kill, a replica can fall too far behind to catch up from the log. It then needs a snapshot install: a full copy of the data from the leader.

SoakWhat happenedFix
First, November 4A restarted replica could not rejoin. Its install took 53 to 130 seconds instead of 4 to 24. The leader kept sending log entries that the replica could not apply, about 2 million during one install, and the node ran out of memory at every limit we tried.Kommander refuses these entries during an install. Kahuna times each install phase and releases the old state before it builds the new state.
Second, November 4No node died, but one install took 205 seconds, and 174 of them were in a step that waited with no deadline. The leader also removed 2.4 million log entries that the replica still needed, so a second install followed. With only two voting replicas left, a 30-second pause of the leader became a 29-second outage.Kahuna removes that wait from the install. Kommander keeps the log entries until the install ends, and waits 10 minutes before it removes a dead member.
Third, November 5After a 2-minute kill of the leader, the new leader's connection to the returned node stayed broken for 53 minutes, with about 45,000 log lines per minute. With the third voting replica down, the two survivors kept repeating elections. The cause was a timing defect in the .NET gRPC client.Kommander moves to a gRPC version with the upstream fix, replaces a connection that stays failed for 30 seconds, and limits the log lines.

The balance checks passed in the first two runs, so those defects cost availability and recovery time, not data. The first defect needs a store that is about an hour old, and a ten-minute run never has one. The third needs a timeout to fire in a narrow gap between two connection attempts. Hand-written tests rarely reach states like these. Later soaks on the fixed versions confirmed all of these fixes.

Limits of these numbers​

  • High volume covers few shapes. Millions of transfers over 2,000 rows repeat one shape many times. The nightly jobs and the fuzzer exist to reach other shapes.
  • Most of the soak volume has a simple check. The soak checks totals and row ledgers. The stronger Elle check applies to the nightly histories, about 5 million transactions per night.
  • This is not a production cluster. These runs use one self-hosted machine or shared CI machines. They say little about a large table, a database larger than memory, or a real network between regions.

Edge cases, planned tests, and public harnesses​

These tests catch regressions and find new edge cases. An edge case might appear only once in 2 million transactions, so a short test run rarely meets it.

The tests cannot prove that CamusDB has no bugs. A green run says only that these checks found no defect in these runs.

We plan to add new test shapes that exercise the database from other angles, with a wider range of scenarios and combinations of features.

The nightly runs are public on GitHub, and the harnesses are open: Caraxes, Kahuna Jepsen and Kommander Jepsen. You can read the scenarios and run them against your own build.

item.title: What a SQL fuzzer catches
item.description: How the CamusDB SQL fuzzer finds wrong rows with no error, without a second database, and which defects it can catch in the future.
item.content:encoded:
This post shows how the CamusDB SQL fuzzer finds queries that return the wrong rows with no error, which defects it can catch, and what it cannot see. A hand-written test covers the cases its author thought of. The fuzzer generates cases nobody wrote, and it runs every night on its own. You need no knowledge of fuzzers or of database internals.

A fuzzer that needs no second database​

A fuzzer makes random inputs and feeds them to the software under test. For a database, the inputs are tables, rows and SQL statements. The hard part is to know the correct answer of a random query.

One way is to run the same query on a second database, for example PostgreSQL, and compare the two answers. That needs a second database, and the two must agree on every rule of SQL. The CamusDB fuzzer takes another way: it checks that two different queries give the same answer, with no need to know the correct one. The name for this is a metamorphic test. Each such rule is an oracle.

Here is an example. SQL has three truth values: a filter on a row is true, false or unknown, and unknown comes from NULL. So the rows where a filter is true, the rows where it is false and the rows where it is unknown add up to the whole table. The fuzzer runs the four queries and checks the sum. If the results do not agree, one of them is wrong. The fuzzer does not need to know which one.

The oracles are the ones of SQLancer, an open tool for database tests, written again in C#. They run in the same process as the engine, with no driver, no network and no second database.

The five steps of a round​

The fuzzer works in rounds. Each round does five things:

  1. It makes a random schema: a few tables with columns of mixed types, and some indexes.
  2. It fills the tables with random rows, NULL values included.
  3. It makes a random statement, for example a query with a join and a filter.
  4. It hands the statement to one oracle. The oracle makes its variants and runs them all on the engine.
  5. It compares the results.

A disagreement is a finding. The fuzzer writes it to disk at once, so a later hang cannot lose it. Then it shrinks the finding: it removes tables, rows, columns and parts of the query until the smallest case that still fails remains. Last, it prints the shrunk case as a ready-to-paste unit test, with the seed that replays it.

Every round takes its random numbers from a base seed and a round number. The same two numbers give the same schema, data and statements again. So a finding from the nightly job replays on a developer's machine with one command.

A time limit applies to every statement. A statement past the limit is a finding too. If it does not stop on cancellation, the fuzzer discards the engine and starts a new one.

The defects it can catch​

A plan is the engine's choice of how to run a query: which index to read, in which order to join the tables, and with which join algorithm. Most logic bugs appear in only one plan. So the oracles make the engine take different paths to one answer. The table lists the five oracles, the rule each one enforces, and what a failure would point to.

OracleThe ruleA failure would mean
Error classificationEvery error carries a specific CamusDB error code. Every statement finishes within a time limit. Every result row serializes to the JSON that the HTTP API sends.A raw exception that reaches the client, such as an overflow or a null reference. An internal-error code. A statement that never finishes. A value that no client can receive.
Ternary logic partitioningThe three-way split from above: the rows where a filter is true, false and unknown add up to the rows with no filter. The same holds for MIN, MAX, SUM and COUNT, for DISTINCT, for GROUP BY and HAVING, and for the ON condition of a join.A NULL compared the wrong way. A NaN or a negative zero that is true on one path and false on another. A comparison whose truth value changes with the path.
NoRECThe unoptimized form is the reference: COUNT(*) with a filter equals SUM(CASE WHEN filter THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) with no filter. The first form lets the planner use indexes. The second form tests the filter on every row of a full scan.An index seek with wrong bounds. A lookup that loses a key. A filter pushed to the wrong side of a join.
Plan equivalenceOne query returns the same rows under every plan: each index choice, each join algorithm, the heuristic planner, the spill-to-disk join, the plan cache, and both row decoders. The oracle reads the EXPLAIN of both plans to confirm that they differ.An index or a join algorithm that returns other rows than a plain scan. A cached plan that gives wrong rows on its second use. A join that drops a row when it spills to disk.
DML integrityAfter each INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or UPSERT, the table holds exactly what the rule expects: the affected-row count, each value, no extra row, no lost row. The row store, every index and the values stored outside their rows agree. A failed statement changes nothing. In a transaction, one failure aborts the whole transaction.Twin rows. An index entry with no row, or a row with no index entry. A column copy inside an index that did not follow an update. A lost out-of-row value. A wrong affected-row count. An UPSERT that skipped its insert or its update. A failed write that changed data.

A FLOAT64 sum gets a tolerance, because the order of the additions changes a float sum. Every other value compares exactly.

Defects outside its reach​

A metamorphic oracle finds results that disagree. It does not find a result that is wrong in the same way on every path. If every form of a query computes the same wrong value, the comparison passes. Such defects need a reference, for example PostgreSQL or an in-memory model. The generator is built for that: it makes statement trees, not SQL text, and a second printer can turn the same trees into another dialect.

The fuzzer runs one session at a time. It does not find concurrency bugs, isolation anomalies or bugs that need an injected fault. Other harnesses own those. The row oracles skip queries whose rows depend on order: LIMIT, window functions and set operations. Those forms still run under the error oracle, but nothing checks their rows.

Run the fuzzer locally​

dotnet test CamusDB.SqlFuzz.Tests/CamusDB.SqlFuzz.Tests.csproj --filter "FullyQualifiedName~.FuzzCampaignTests."

This runs all five oracles for 30 seconds each, with a seed from the clock. SQLFUZZ_SEED fixes the seed, and SQLFUZZ_BUDGET_SECONDS sets the time per oracle. A failed run prints the seed, the round and a unit test that reproduces the finding. The full guide is docs/sql-fuzzer.md in the CamusDB repository.

Coverage that hand-written tests miss​

A hand-written test checks one schema, one data set and one query. The fuzzer makes a new schema, a new data set and new statements in every round, and each night starts from a new seed. It reaches the shapes nobody writes by hand: a NULL in a join key, an index on a column with one distinct value, an UPDATE that changes every column of an index at once.

This makes the two systems at the heart of CamusDB more robust. The query system must return the same rows under every plan, and the fuzzer forces every plan. The write system must leave rows, indexes and out-of-row values in agreement after every statement. The fuzzer checks that agreement after every write. A night with no finding is evidence that both rules hold. A finding arrives as a small failing test, before a user meets the same defect in production.

A change inside the engine joins the test on its first night. A new join algorithm, a new index path or a new row decoder needs no new test. The same statements run, and the oracles judge the new path as before.

item.title: Introducing SolariumDB: Taking Control of the Storage Layer in .NET
item.description: SolariumDB is an embedded key-value storage engine written entirely in C#, built to give CamusDB end-to-end control of the storage layer in .NET.
item.content:encoded:
This post introduces SolariumDB, an embedded key-value storage engine written entirely in C#. You will see why we built it, how it compares with RocksDB in our first benchmarks, and where it fits in the CamusDB stack. RocksDB stays the default storage engine of CamusDB.

With SolariumDB, you can debug the storage engine of your database with the same tools you use for your .NET applications. It brings us one step closer to a database built entirely in .NET, from the SQL layer down to the code that writes data to disk.

RocksDB is hard to inspect from .NET​

SolariumDB is different from CamusDB. It is a storage engine: the layer that persists data, organizes files, manages memory, and recovers after failures. It is an embedded library: it runs inside another program and has no server of its own.

SolariumDB follows the architecture of RocksDB, a Log-Structured Merge Tree (LSM-tree). It has four parts:

  • Write-ahead log (WAL): a file that records each write before it is applied, for recovery after a crash.
  • Memtable: the newest writes, held sorted in memory.
  • SSTables: immutable sorted files on disk, written when a memtable is full and organized in levels.
  • Compaction: a background task that merges SSTables and removes old data.

RocksDB is a mature and reliable storage engine. It is the default backend for CamusDB, and we have no plans to change that soon.

However, RocksDB is native code. We can profile our C# code, but to follow an operation into the storage engine we need a different set of tools. We also have limited control over its internal I/O behavior unless we modify RocksDB itself.

Five advantages of a storage engine in C#​

  • End-to-end debugging and profiling. We can follow an operation from the application down to the storage layer with .NET tools.
  • Direct control over I/O. Every file operation goes through an abstraction we control. That lets us experiment with io_uring, an asynchronous I/O interface of Linux, and with other I/O strategies.
  • Workload-specific optimizations. We can tune storage behavior for the applications that use it, in addition to general-purpose defaults.
  • Better observability. We can expose internal metrics such as write stalls, pending compactions, memtable usage, and file activity.
  • No native dependencies. The storage engine ships as .NET assemblies, with no separate native binaries for each platform.

SolariumDB was first designed around the Raft log of Kommander, and it also serves as a storage backend for Kahuna.

One example of a workload-specific optimization: Raft logs are mostly append-only and periodically discard old entries. SolariumDB can move SSTables that do not overlap between levels with no rewrite of their contents, which reduces disk I/O.

Benchmark results against RocksDB​

In our October 29 benchmarks, SolariumDB achieved up to 2.8 times RocksDB's throughput in unsynced Kommander WAL workloads. Unsynced means that a write returns before the data is forced to the disk. Synced writes generally performed similarly, because the storage device limited both engines.

In Kahuna's larger dataset, served from the operating system's page cache, SolariumDB achieved approximately 1.8 times the read throughput of RocksDB configured to use buffered reads with eight reader threads.

These results come from specific workloads on a single machine. We do not claim that SolariumDB is faster in general.

Some areas need work:

  • Garbage collection can affect tail latency (the slowest operations) under heavy load.
  • Some compaction workloads need better tuning.
  • The io_uring implementation does not outperform the default I/O path in every scenario.

The results show that a storage engine written in C# can have competitive performance.

The complete methodology and results are in our benchmarks.

CamusDB supports several storage engines​

CamusDB was designed to support multiple storage backends, as MySQL does, where you select a storage engine for your requirements. Some workloads need write throughput, others need efficient range scans, and others need predictable latency under heavy concurrency.

Interchangeable storage engines let us explore those tradeoffs with no rebuild of the whole database.

Other databases took this approach. CockroachDB replaced RocksDB with Pebble, a storage engine written in Go, partly to gain more control over its implementation and optimization. SolariumDB has a similar motivation within the .NET ecosystem.

The five projects under CamusDB​

Each project came from a specific need during the work on CamusDB. Each one can be used independently, and together they make a distributed database.

  • CamusDB: Distributed SQL database
  • Kahuna: Distributed key-value store, node scaling, backups, etc.
  • Kommander: Raft, WAL, leader election and balancing, consensus, etc.
  • Nixie: High-performance actor model
  • Solarium: Embedded key-value store, handling the low-level disk I/O

This is how they fit together inside CamusDB:

CamusDB turns SQL into key-value operations on Kahuna. Inside Kahuna, Nixie actors handle concurrency: each key and lock belongs to one single-threaded actor, so Kahuna avoids sharing mutable state between threads. Kahuna replicates its writes through Kommander. On each node, a storage engine writes both the key-value state and the Raft log to disk. Today that engine is RocksDB by default, and SolariumDB is the alternative.

RocksDB stays the default​

SolariumDB is still young and has not yet proven itself in production.

RocksDB will remain CamusDB's default storage engine while we continue to test, benchmark, and harden SolariumDB for durability, recovery, and predictable behavior. Our goal is to mature SolariumDB into a strong alternative.

item.title: From 400 to 10,000 operations per second in CamusDB
item.description: What helped a three-node CamusDB cluster reach 10K ops/sec on one laptop, and how to interpret the result.
item.content:encoded:
If you're investigating database throughput, our experience offers a practical place to look: the work repeated around every query and commit. Here's what we removed, how we measured the gains, and what the resulting benchmark can tell you about CamusDB.

Many months ago, when we first started measuring database throughput in cluster mode, we discovered it could only handle around 400 ops/sec. After a long journey of benchmarking, investigating bottlenecks, and optimizing the system, we've reached 10K ops/sec.

On October 12, a three-node cluster sustained 10,284 durable operations per second for 45 minutes, completing 27.8 million operations after a two-minute warm-up. Every measured minute stayed above 9,700 ops/sec.

All three nodes ran on one laptop, alongside the load generator and metrics collector, on memory-backed storage. Both conditions limit what the number predicts; see Latency and scope of the result.

Definition of an operation​

We used Caraxes, our database testing tool, to run a bank ledger with 2,000 accounts. Half the operations read one account by its primary key. The other half transferred money: subtract from one account, add to another, and commit both changes together.

The read operation executes this parameterized query. @id is the account's primary key; the client consumes all four returned columns and checks that the requested account came back before counting the read as complete.

SELECT id, balance, version, payload
FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @id;

A transfer moves one unit between two distinct accounts. The sequential client visits them in ascending row-index order, reading and updating each in turn. Here is the sequence, with parameter names expanded to distinguish the two accounts:

BEGIN;

/* account 1 */
SELECT balance, version FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @low_id;
UPDATE workload_accounts
SET balance = @low_balance, version = version + 1 WHERE id = @low_id;

/* account 2 */
SELECT balance, version FROM workload_accounts WHERE id = @high_id;
UPDATE workload_accounts
SET balance = @high_balance, version = version + 1 WHERE id = @high_id;

COMMIT;

The client calculates each new balance from the value it read: subtract one from the sender and add one to the recipient. Either account can be the sender. Each update must match exactly one row, and incrementing version lets the verifier account for row changes afterward. The driver starts and commits the transaction through its API; BEGIN and COMMIT show those boundaries here.

One committed transfer counts as one operation, including both reads, both updates, and the commit. The result was approximately 5,140 standalone reads and 5,145 committed transfers per second.

Transfers selected accounts across the whole table, so concurrent transactions could modify the same rows. Conflicting work was retried. The run used read-committed isolation and 256 concurrent workers over 64 connections; each worker waited for its operation to finish before starting another.

Afterward, Caraxes reconciled the ledger. The total balance was unchanged, and no transaction had an indeterminate outcome: none left the client unsure whether it committed.

Three replicas, one hardware budget​

The host was an Intel Core i7-13620H laptop with 10 cores, 16 hardware threads, and 31 GiB of RAM, running Debian 12 and Docker.

The table had one replication group: a leader that ordered writes and two followers that maintained their own copies.

Every write goes through consensus: nodes agree on the ordered changes before those changes reach database storage. Some reads also require consensus coordination. Each write is stored three times, once per node. All that work competes for the same machine's resources.

The laptop's consumer NVMe drive changed its write behavior after roughly 30 GB of sustained writes.

Changes that produced the gains​

Send requests directly to the leader. Initially, the client could contact any node, which might forward the request. Teaching it which node led the data range removed that extra hop and produced a 1.97× improvement.

Reduce the cost of agreement. CamusDB uses Raft, a protocol for keeping replicas in agreement. Improvements to replication and follower queues reduced a replication round from about 2.31 ms to 1.56 ms, adding 8–9% in throughput. Briefly collecting writes into batches also helped several requests share replication work. Measuring the actual wait and wake-up time was essential; the configured delay alone did not describe the cost.

Write fewer log entries. Replicas record changes in a log so they can apply them in order. A change in Kahuna, the transactional storage layer under CamusDB, reduced the log entries per transfer from six to four. That removed work from the replication path for every committed transfer.

Schedule less work. Some storage reads could use a published snapshot of the latest state without entering a queue for the key. More targeted notifications also reduced scheduling overhead. Together, these changes cut thread-pool work items from 65 to 33 per client operation. A thread pool runs queued pieces of work; making it schedule fewer pieces left more CPU time for the operations themselves.

Avoid repeating primary-key lookups. A primary-key lookup first finds the row's internal identifier. Caching that identifier let later requests skip the index read. This reduced underlying storage reads per operation by 47% and CPU time per operation by 8%. The cache recorded 76.85 million hits, no misses after warm-up, and no stale identifiers during the run.

Increasing concurrency from 128 to 256 workers then added another 8% in throughput. Latency roughly doubled, while CPU cost per operation stayed unchanged. More concurrency helped use the capacity we had freed, with a clear cost to individual requests.

Changes that did not help​

Several plausible changes failed to improve the result. Setting the .NET thread-pool minimum to 64, 128, or 1,024 made no measurable difference. Client TLS showed no measurable CPU cost at the leader. Sending transaction requests through a pipelined client at 128 workers did not help either.

Those measurements narrowed the investigation. We could stop tuning those settings and focus on costs that moved throughput or CPU time per operation.

Latency and scope of the result​

The final run's median read latency was 3.6 ms, with 99% completing within 18 ms. Median transfer latency was 36 ms, with 99% within 157 ms. Throughput needs those latency numbers beside it, especially when increasing concurrency makes individual operations slower.

The leader was the bottleneck, consuming about 8.5 CPU cores; each follower used roughly 1.53. Three separate machines would provide a different resource budget and add network latency between replicas. This run cannot predict that deployment's throughput.

The 2,000-row working set also fits comfortably in memory. It stresses transaction processing and contention, without measuring large-table scans or a database larger than RAM. Client traffic used cleartext gRPC; traffic between Raft peers retained certificate protection.

Correctness was checked beyond the throughput run. The same stack passed two two-hour fault tests involving killed leaders, paused processes, and severely throttled disks. Balances remained correct, replicas did not diverge, and no transactions remained unresolved across the tested restarts. The separate NVMe fault tests measured 3,230–5,485 ops/sec under their conditions.

The frozen campaign baseline was 407.86 ops/sec with the same workload shape and 32 workers. The final result is 25.2× higher, combining software changes with increased concurrency. It is a milestone for this workload and setup.

If you're profiling your own system, count the forwarding hops, log entries, queued tasks, and lookups behind each operation, and run correctness checks to confirm that the faster system still does the right work.

Result on shared commodity hardware​

Running three nodes on a single machine with commodity hardware is far from ideal and certainly not a recommended practice, since the shared hardware becomes a single point of failure for all three nodes. However, it demonstrates that even under these challenging conditions, the database can deliver performance that is more than adequate for the vast majority of transactional applications.

item.title: Six planner changes for many-table joins, measured with the Join Order Benchmark
item.content:encoded:
If your queries join five, ten or fifteen tables, CamusDB now plans them better and runs them faster. This post explains what changed in plain terms, so you can see what to expect from your own queries.

A join query names its tables and its conditions. It does not say in which order to join the tables. The database picks the order, and the order decides how much data the query reads. A good order starts from the few rows that survive the filters. A bad order can build millions of rows and then throw most of them away.

The Join Order Benchmark (JOB) is a set of 113 queries from a 2015 paper by Leis and five co-authors. The queries run over a movie database of 21 tables, and each one joins 4 to 17 tables. The paper tested mature databases and found that their estimates of how many rows a join returns were often wrong by orders of magnitude. The error grows with each join, and a wrong estimate leads to a slow plan. The benchmark exists to show that weakness.

First run: 25 of 113 queries timed out​

In July I wrote about how CamusDB searches for a join order. In short, the planner finds the cheapest plan for small groups of tables first and reuses those plans for larger groups.

Our first run of the 113 JOB queries used synthetic movie data at 1/1000 of the real size. SQLite ran the same rows as an independent check. Every CamusDB result matched. But 25 queries did not finish in 30 seconds, and the full run took 1,159 seconds. Every plan contained a cross product, a join of every row against every row.

The executor was fine. We put the tables of two queries in a good order by hand. One query went from 10 seconds to 0.4 seconds. Another went from a timeout to 40 milliseconds. The planner did not find the order on its own.

Six planner changes​

Six changes made the difference. Each one stands on its own and applies to every join query, including queries outside the benchmark.

The planner reads every condition on its own. A JOB query lists its tables with commas and puts all conditions in WHERE. The old planner grouped the conditions as the query wrote them. A table whose only link came through a later table looked unconnected, so the planner joined it with a cross product. The planner now reads each condition on its own and finds the links between tables wherever they are. No JOB plan has a cross product today. The run went from 1,159 seconds to 184 seconds, with no timeouts.

One estimate per group of tables. To compare two orders, the planner estimates how many rows each step produces. JOB queries name the same movie through up to six columns and write every pair of them as equal. The old estimator treated each of those fifteen equalities as a separate filter and multiplied the estimate down to almost nothing. The new estimator sees one fact: these six columns hold the same value. The run went from 184 seconds to 9.5 seconds.

Wide joins get the full search. The search compares every group of tables that an order can build. That number grows fast, so the old search stopped at 12 tables and used a simple rule above that. Nine JOB queries have 14 or 17 tables. The search now skips the groups that no order can build, which are most of them, and plans joins of up to 30 tables. Past a budget of steps it takes a fast greedy order instead of a slow search.

Statistics that see popular values. The planner sizes a join from the number of distinct values in the join column. That formula assumes every value is as common as every other. Real data is not like that: one movie has thousands of cast rows and most have a few. ANALYZE now keeps the most common values of each column with their counts, and the planner uses them. It also records how many rows hold NULL, because a NULL key joins with nothing. When a query filters a small lookup table down to one row, the planner reads that row before it plans. It then prices the join by the popularity of that key.

Each lookup costs less. With a good order, a join runs as a chain of index lookups. For each row on the left, the join finds the rows on the right that match. The old lookup asked the store for a page of 512 index entries and used 11 of them on average. The lookup now stops at the entries of its key. The join also keeps the rows of each key it found, so a repeated key costs nothing. And it sends a page of left rows to the store in one request instead of one request per row.

A test that watches plan quality. A correctness test does not catch a planner that returns the right rows and reads ten times more data to do it. A new test suite runs a fixed set of queries on fixed data and counts the rows and lookups of each plan. It compares the counts with a baseline file in git and fails when a query's work grows by more than half. The JOB queries run every night, and every result is checked against SQLite.

Benchmark results​

Work is the number of rows read, key lookups and index entries scanned over the whole plan, at a scale of about 225,000 rows.

BaselineTotal work, 113 queriesLargest estimate error
First baseline6,111,33678,378x
Current1,007,7521,240x

The engine does one sixth of the work it did at the first baseline, for the same results. The same test on the same laptop ran the 113 queries in 51 seconds before the lookup changes and runs them in 7.9 seconds today. No query takes more than a second. The three 17-table queries took 4 to 5 seconds each and now run in under 15 milliseconds.

The plan quality page in the docs compares the three engines on the same rows with warm runs. CamusDB takes 1.5 seconds, SQLite 7.2 seconds and PostgreSQL 0.74 seconds. CamusDB runs as an embedded node on a transactional key-value store, so read these times as a reference point. Before this work, 25 of these queries did not finish at all.

Effect on queries outside the benchmark​

Each change answers a problem that real tables have. The benchmark only made them visible at the same time.

The shape of a JOB query is common. One large table links to many small ones, and the filters sit on the small ones. That is a star schema, and most applications have one:

  • An online store joins orders to customers, products, categories, warehouses and shipments. A report filters on one category or one month.
  • A ledger joins transactions to accounts, counterparties, currencies and instruments. A statement filters on one account and a date range.
  • A multi-tenant product joins events to tenants, users, projects and plans. Every query filters on one tenant.
  • A game backend joins players, inventories, items, trades and guilds. A player's screen filters on one player.

The data behind those tables is skewed, has NULLs, and repeats its keys:

  • A few products appear in most orders. A few accounts hold most of the transactions. One tenant can hold half of the rows. A planner that prices every value alike plans for the average and then meets the largest customer.
  • Foreign keys are often NULL: an order without a coupon, a transaction without a counterparty, an item without an owner. An estimate that ignores NULLs is wrong by the NULL share.
  • Keys repeat. Every line of an order carries the same order id, and every row of an inventory carries the same owner. A lookup that remembers its answers runs once per key.
  • Nobody writes a FROM list in the best order, and an ORM or a report builder writes it in no order at all. The planner has to find it.

The last point matters most for CamusDB. The store is distributed, so each lookup can be a network round trip. A plan that looks up a thousand times where ten would do is slow by the latency of the cluster.

Six properties of a robust optimizer​

These six properties keep the optimizer robust outside the benchmark:

  1. Results never change. SQLite checks every plan on every nightly run. A plan that changes results is a bug.
  2. The search is bounded. The step budget and the greedy fallback keep planning time small at any width. The 17-table queries plan in 9 to 16 milliseconds.
  3. The same query gets the same plan. Two orders of equal cost keep the order the user wrote.
  4. Missing statistics lead to a fallback order. Without statistics the planner uses a simple order and still removes avoidable cross products.
  5. The plan is visible. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows the order the search chose, its estimate next to the actual rows, and the lookups each join saved.
  6. Regressions are caught before merge. The plan quality test runs on every pull request.

Remaining gaps​

PostgreSQL executes the corpus five times faster, and the gap is in the executor, not in the planner. The search considers one shape of plan, a chain that adds one table at a time. Plans that join two groups of tables, and a search below an outer join, are not there yet. The worst estimate error is still above 1,000x on one query.

item.title: What the dragon found, part three: a two-hour fault test
item.description: A dragon breaking one artic city of glowing pyramids
item.content:encoded:
This post reports what a two-hour fault test found in CamusDB over three weeks: nodes that ran out of memory, a partition with no leader, a replica that lost rows, and two lost writes on local builds. You will see each defect, its fix, and the state of the database after them. If you are evaluating CamusDB, it shows the evidence behind its behavior in long runs with faults.

Part one introduced Caraxes, the tool that attacks a real CamusDB cluster in Docker. Part two told what it found in its first month.

Most of this part is about one test. It runs for two hours, it injects a fault every eight minutes, and it took eight attempts before it passed. Every failed attempt found something, and the runs after the first pass kept finding things.

Commits and releases in three weeks​

CamusDB still runs on two lower layers. Kahuna is the replicated key-value store under the SQL engine. Kommander is the Raft implementation under Kahuna. A chaos run attacks all three at once.

Some terms in this post:

  • Raft: the protocol with which nodes agree on the order of writes. Each partition of the data has one leader that accepts writes and followers that copy its log. An election round is a term, and the nodes that vote are voters.
  • Backfill, snapshot install, and re-seed: a leader sends missing log entries to a follower that is behind (backfill). If those entries no longer exist, it sends a full copy of the state in chunks (snapshot install, or re-seed).
  • Intent: a write of a transaction that has not settled yet.
  • Wedge: a partition or a key that stops making progress and does not recover by itself.
  • Soak: a long test run. A soak often runs as two arms: two runs that differ in one setting.
  • Elle and Jepsen: open tools that check a history of operations for consistency anomalies.
RepositoryCommits since 2026-09-21Versions consumed by CamusDB
CamusDB116
Kahuna100from 1.9.2 to 1.11.10
Kommander68from 1.7.6 to 1.10.9
Caraxes25
.NET client26

Caraxes now has 332 scenario files, up from about 200. More than thirty of the runs in this period were two hours long. That is more than sixty hours of a cluster under attack, on one host, with the same seed.

The two-hour soak and its pass conditions​

Every ten-minute scenario in part two passed on the stack we shipped at the time. In those runs, node memory climbed to between 3.3 and 3.9 GB of a 4 GiB limit within ten minutes and then stayed there. Whether that plateau holds for two hours, or creeps, is a question no ten-minute run can answer. Snapshot installs, log compaction and retention floors are also things that only start to matter when the log is tens of millions of entries long.

So we wrote the soak. Three nodes with 4 GiB each, one partition replicated three times, the bank workload from part two with 128 workers over 2,000 rows, and a two-hour measured window. Fourteen faults land one every eight minutes. Six of them kill the current leader and restart it 30 seconds later. Four freeze a process for 30 seconds. Four pause one node's disk at 4 KiB per second for 30 seconds.

nemesis:
  seed: 1
  events:
    - { at: 8m,   fault: kill,      target: leader, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 16m,  fault: slow-disk, target: camus1, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 24m,  fault: kill,      target: leader, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 32m,  fault: pause,     target: camus2, duration: 30s }
    # ... fourteen windows in all ...
    - { at: 104m, fault: pause,     target: leader, duration: 30s }
    - { at: 112m, fault: kill,      target: leader, duration: 30s }

A soak passes when all of these hold:

  • The window completes, and no node dies on its own.
  • The sum of all balances is exactly 2,993,071,553 at the end, the same number as in part two.
  • Every indeterminate write is resolved. An indeterminate write is a commit whose answer the client never received, because the connection was cut while the commit travelled. The ledger resolves them afterwards: the sum of all row versions must land inside a band whose floor is the committed writes and whose ceiling adds the indeterminate ones.
  • The per-row ledger, joined against the seeded data, names no lost, missing, duplicated or half-applied row.
  • No two replicas applied the same log entry with different verdicts.
  • Every fault window recovers, and the cluster makes progress inside every window.

The soak does not grade throughput. The host's NVMe changes regime after 30 to 35 GB of writes, as part two explained, and a two-hour run always crosses that line. The harness marks a throughput finding inadmissible when the device moved inside the window, and most windows after minute 30 are. The verdict rests on the correctness checks, which do not depend on the device.

Since late September every soak runs as a pair. One arm has the new settle path on, where a transaction's resolved values are installed on every replica when the transaction settles. The other arm has it off, so a replica can keep a reference to the intent and fill in the value later. We call those by-reference records. The settle path writes 4.0 Raft entries per commit instead of 6.4, and it is the default today. Both arms must pass.

Run one: two nodes died of allocator memory​

The first soak completed its window: 17.9 million operations in two hours. It also finished with one node alive, and the reconciliation could not read the sum.

The first node died at minute 51. It was the leader, it was killed on schedule, it restarted, and it ran out of memory while it deserialized the backfill from the new leader. The runtime terminated it on purpose, with a message that said the orchestrator would restart it. Nothing did, because the harness only restarts a node as part of a kill fault, and that fault had already healed. The second node died after the window closed, while the reconciliation tried to read the sum from a two-node cluster. It was at 99.6 percent of its memory limit, with no trace and no dump. The kernel killed it.

It took four runs to find what the memory was.

SuspectTestResult
Transaction record retention. The heap valve logged 185,064 resident records.Read the node metricsThe retention stores peaked at 117 to 131 MB per node, about 3 percent of the container, and held flat. Wrong.
RocksDB block cache and memtablesfs2: one shared budget of 768 MiB for both storage enginesNative memory unchanged at about 3 GB per node. A node died at minute 36, earlier than before. Wrong.
Index and filter blocks of the Raft log, kept outside every cacheMeasured at 8.9 percent of live SST bytes in a probe. Fixed in Kommander, with new gauges. fs3.Table readers read 0 MB. Native memory still 3,069 MB. The live SST was 262 MB, not the 34 GB the ratio implied. Wrong.
glibc malloc arenasRead the process maps on a live node116 anonymous mappings of 60 to 70 MB each, 1,227 MB resident. The process ran 133 threads on 16 cores, right at the allocator's ceiling of eight arenas per core.

glibc is the C library under .NET on Linux. Its allocator keeps a memory arena per thread, and freed memory stays in the arena. It does not return to the kernel. No subsystem gauge could find that memory, because it was not any subsystem's live data.

The fourth soak ran with one environment variable added, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2. The 60 MB mappings fell from 116 to 7.

Nodefs3 peakfs4 peak
camus14,095 MiB, 100%3,463 MiB, 85%
camus24,000 MiB, 98%2,947 MiB, 72%
camus33,957 MiB, 97%3,268 MiB, 80%

No node died. Memory came down between faults, with no creep. Three soaks died of this, and the remedy was a deployment variable, with no change in either codebase. The fix for the Raft log's index blocks stays anyway. It bounded an allocation that had no bound, and its gauges are what made the measurement possible.

One native memory table from the first run says why the first diagnosis was wrong. On the node that died last, the working set grew from 382 MB to 4,057 MB over two hours, while the managed heap shrank from 767 MB to 441 MB. The growth was outside the memory that the garbage collector manages.

A partition with no leader for 59 minutes​

With the deaths out of the way, the fourth soak showed a worse defect.

An hour into the window, with no fault active, client throughput went from 2,160 operations per second to zero in one second. It stayed at zero for 59 minutes. All three nodes were alive and answered every health probe.

All three voters shared a hole in their Raft log. The log was contiguous through entry 48,266,403, and entries were present up to 48,266,486. Neither recovery path could get past the hole:

  • One node won a term and refused to lead on the hole guard. It did that 598 times.
  • Another node won a term and its promotion barrier timed out. It reverted 297 times.
  • The third node never led. Terms climbed to 614. One node logged that the leader could not be resolved 167,244 times.

The trigger was a transient disk stall on one follower that cleared in seconds. The wedge outlived it by an hour.

The defect was known. The Kommander Jepsen suite found it in August, and its findings file recorded 90 nightly runs since then without a reproduction. This was its first reproduction outside Jepsen, on a far newer build, from ordinary device jitter, with no injected fault. The soak also carried two details the Jepsen runs did not have. The refusal counter reset on every promotion attempt, so the truncation escape hatch could never fire. And 296 of the 297 barrier timeouts named no cause, while the real obstacle was the shared hole. Kommander 1.7.7 fixed it, and the next soak had no wedge.

A replica that rejoined with fewer rows​

The fifth soak ran on the published Kommander 1.7.7. No wedge, no node death, peak memory 55 percent. And the cluster stopped before minute 50 anyway, with all three nodes alive.

Minutes0-1010-2020-3030-4040-5050-6060-7070-9090-120
Ops/s5,0864,3102,2254,4801,7555943031-85

The leader was killed at minute 24 and rejoined. The new leader escalated to a snapshot install, and chunk 22 of 23 was rejected after a 16-second install. Within 41 seconds the node's checkpoint jumped ahead of the gap. The retry at that index was answered "already covered, nothing was imported".

From then on, that node held committed values for fewer rows than its peers at the same applied log position: 1,828 rows, then 1,777, then 1,756 of 2,000. Kahuna's fingerprint probe caught the difference three times at error level. The probe only logged, so the node was elected leader twice with the incomplete state. It also kept 172 prepared intents that the other two replicas settled long before. Under retention pressure those intents lost their records, and recovery must hold a record-less intent forever. 86 transactions' keys went read-only, workers piled onto them, and every full-table scan failed its page budget. The reconciliation could not read the table.

The sixth soak, on Kahuna 1.9.7 and Kommander 1.7.9, showed the same defect on a different node, after a snapshot install that completed cleanly with no chunk rejected. So the loss survives a clean install. The seventh soak ran a local Kommander fix for the skip. Same divergence, after two full installs, and this time no kill was involved: the leader stepped down on its own during a disk stall, with a hole in its own log.

Three Kommander changes closed it:

  1. A skip must deliver the committed entries below the index, or it must become an install.
  2. The installer skips the import when the application already applied past the index. An import there rewound state below the apply cursor, and those entries were never re-delivered.
  3. The leader does not escalate to a snapshot for a peer that already reports committed through the checkpoint.

The eighth soak passed.
