It was the first complete, clean two-hour window: conservation exact, 2,912 indeterminate writes all resolved, zero divergence, all fourteen windows recovered in at most 0.8 seconds. The ninth soak repeated it on published packages, Kahuna 1.9.9 and Kommander 1.8.0. That run is stronger evidence than the eighth, because it hit the exact shapes that wedged runs five to seven three times. One node went through a rejected chunk, a forced install and a 24-chunk re-install, and was then elected leader three times with no divergence and no held intents.

Kahuna 1.9.11 then added containment. A replica whose apply projection diverges from its peers is gated: it gives up leadership, withholds its candidacy, and is re-seeded. Live intents are part of the fingerprint now, and a record-less hold is cross-checked with peers. The tenth soak passed with the containment in the build. It did not fire, because there was nothing to contain.

RunStackResultWhat it found
fs1Kahuna 1.9.3, Kommander 1.7.6Two nodes dead, no verdictNative memory grew while the managed heap shrank
fs2Same, with a 768 MiB storage budgetOne node dead at minute 36Not the block cache
fs3Raft log index blocks charged to the cacheOne node dead at minute 85, sum exactNot the table readers. Allocator arenas.
fs4MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2No deaths. Leaderless for 59 minutes.Three voters shared one hole in the log
fs5Kahuna 1.9.4, Kommander 1.7.7Read-only wedge by minute 50A replica rejoined with about 10 percent of its rows behind, and led twice
fs6Kahuna 1.9.7, Kommander 1.7.9SameThe loss survives a clean install
fs7Local Kommander skip fixSame, with no kill involvedAn import below the apply cursor rewound state
fs8Three Kommander changes, localPassThe first clean two hours
fs9Kahuna 1.9.9, Kommander 1.8.0PassRepair paths exercised three times, no divergence
fs10Kahuna 1.9.11, Kommander 1.8.2PassContainment in the build, silent

Seven more findings after the first pass​

We ran the soak again on every new stack after it passed, and it found more. None of them was a lost write on a published package. Several of them were one step away from it.

A candidate that discarded valid votes. The eleventh soak paused the leader's process for 30 seconds, and the cluster completed zero operations for all 30. One survivor campaigned in terms 72 through 78. The other granted its vote every time. The candidate discarded every grant, because it re-checked the voter's log by index only, while the voter judged by term and index. Each grant also put the voter into its post-vote cooldown, so it never campaigned itself. The partition had no leader until the paused node woke up. The same discarded-vote line appeared 4 times in fs9 and zero times in fs8 and fs10, so the condition depends on timing and a soak alone cannot prove it gone. Kommander now judges a grant by the voter's own rule, and a deterministic test holds the shape.

A veto that arrived late. One error line grew with every build: 2 or 3 per node in fs3, 21 in fs8, 47 in fs9, 78 distinct transactions in fs10. The ledger found zero lost writes every time, so it sat on the watch list. The cause was a prepare re-driven to a successor after a step-down. Its first copy had already settled, and the re-driven copy installed a phantom intent that the fence then refused against the transaction's own commit. Kahuna now remembers settled identities from the log, and the count went from 78 to zero.

The faster commit path broke the retention floor. A Kommander change that fans a proposal out before the leader's local write took one fsync out of every round. On this host's device that is 5,292 operations per second against 2,243 on the same body. It also turned the log retention budget of one million entries from 80 seconds of log into 37. A leader killed for 30 seconds came back 1.7 million entries behind, below the compaction floor, and needed a whole-partition transfer. The import ran out of memory. Retention is sized in time as well as entries since Kommander 1.9.2, and that soak passed at 4,235 operations per second, with 6,971 in its first ten minutes before the device changed regime.

An install loop with a 15-second deadline. On Kahuna 1.10.5 a restarted leader entered a snapshot install loop. The last chunk's install took longer than the 15-second acknowledgement deadline on a busy device. The retry started a new export at a new index instead of a resume. The follower rejected the retry while its own install was in progress. Six attempts in four minutes, and the node's memory went from 1.15 GB to 4.08 GB in three and a half minutes, then it crashed. The same loop ran in the previous soak and finished on the second to fourth attempt, with memory at 96.6 percent. The margin was between 100 and 300 MB. The settle-path arm of the same pair landed five of six installs on the first attempt in 8 to 15 seconds, because its snapshot carries fewer intents. A smaller snapshot hid the race.

Lost writes, twice, on local packs. The packs that fixed the loop lost committed writes. In the first run the sum came back short by 4. Two rows were 58 and 180 version increments behind, about 100 seconds of each row's writes. The restarted node received a checkpoint over its replication gap. The leader escalated to a snapshot at exactly that index, the receiver answered "already covered, nothing was imported", and the leader moved its cursors past the gap. The node led one minute later. The entries between its frontier and the boundary never reached its application. In the second run the sum was short by 2, from a different cause. On restart, the node replayed the window below its certified position as history, and 82,536 by-reference records on all 2,000 keys found no intent to resolve against. The values were missing on that one node. The control arm, with the settle path on, on the same packs and the same schedule, passed.

A gate that fired nine minutes late. With the replay fixed, the next soak passed, and one of its six restarts left 10,773 unresolved records on 13 keys. Kahuna's new recovery gate caught it nine minutes later, after the node had won three terms. The node refused to serve, handed leadership to the fuller replica, re-seeded in 19.6 seconds and ungated. No loss. Nine minutes is too long, so the gate now fires at detection, and the next pair passed on both arms with the unresolved counter at zero on six restarts.

A paused follower re-seeded three times. The soak on the published Kahuna 1.11.5 and Kommander 1.10.4 passed on both arms, and both arms showed the same thing. A 30-second pause at minute 104, with 60 to 70 million entries in the log, was followed by three consecutive whole-partition re-seeds: 32, 38 and 31 chunks in 60, 41 and 8 seconds, with the follower at 92 percent of its memory during the first. The first diagnosis said the follower fell below the compaction floor. That was wrong: the retention window covered it by an order of magnitude. The backfill's no-progress probe counted four shipments fruitless because the follower's reported commit frontier did not move, while its presence frontier advanced at 1,100 entries per second against a stream of 6,700. Each install left the follower a million entries behind, and the probe fired again. With the probe reading every frontier, the same pause was repaired by backfill: 92,000 entries behind to 13 in 28 seconds. Kommander 1.10.7 ships it, and in the latest soak the minute-104 pause hit the leader, which caught up from 188,000 entries behind to 3,000 in three minutes with no escalation.

fs12Kommander vote fix, localPass
fs13Kahuna 1.10.1, Kommander 1.9.0Correct. Harness fail.A health probe issued 0.28 s before the kill
r3a6Kommander round pack, localFail: import ran out of memory2.4x the throughput made a 30 s kill fall below the retention floor
rl4bKahuna 1.10.4, Kommander 1.9.2Pass, both armsThe version band had the wrong unit
rl5Kahuna 1.10.5, Kommander 1.9.3Fail: node dead in an install loopA 15 s chunk deadline the last chunk could not meet
sn1Local snapshot packsFail: sum short by 4A skipped install over a gap, then the node led
sn2Local, skip fixedFail: sum short by 2. Control arm passed.Restart replay left 82,536 values unresolved
sn3Local, replay fixedPassThe recovery gate caught 10,773 unresolved records, nine minutes late
sn4Local, gate at detectionPass, both arms
rl6Kahuna 1.11.5, Kommander 1.10.4Pass, both armsA paused follower re-seeded three times in four minutes
ps1Local probe fixPass, both armsThe same pause repaired by backfill in 28 s
rl7Kahuna 1.11.7, Kommander 1.10.7One arm failed a harness ruleA client check on one 1-second sample
rl7bSamePassTwo green verdicts on one published stack

Seven false alarms from the test setup​

Each item below cost us one wrong reading and is now a check, as in the list from part two.

  • Two false reports of a node that died on its own. In one run the health probe was issued 0.28 seconds before the scheduled SIGKILL, and the harness graded the missed probe as a death with no fault active. In another, docker kill took 6.8 seconds to return on a device at 98 percent busy, and the harness opened the fault window when the command returned, seven seconds after the node died. Fault windows now open when the fault is issued, and a probe in flight within its own timeout before a window is excused. Both runs re-grade as passes on recorded data.
  • 801 version increments above the band were the band's unit. One run's version sum exceeded the ceiling that the indeterminate writes allowed. The ceiling counted one row per indeterminate transaction. A transfer increments two rows. With the right unit the sum was inside the band and the excess above the floor was even, so every transfer applied whole. We replayed the corrected band over 410 archived runs. Thirty runs that had read "above the maximum" were inside. One run from August 28, with zero indeterminate writes and a conserved balance, grew the version sum by 8: four transfers applied that the client never committed. The check was waived under faults at the time, and the waiver hid it. The band is graded in bank mode now, and an odd excess fails as a half-applied transfer.
  • An Elle history with holes in it. On Docker Desktop for macOS the workload wrote its history through a bind mount, and every time a fault started a helper container, a page-aligned run of zero bytes appeared in the host copy. Elle could not parse the history, so one scenario never had a verdict. The measured run now writes inside its container and the harness copies the output out.
  • A node-removal fault that removed nothing. The node-removal fault posted its leave request from the host. The request arrived through Docker's port proxy from the bridge gateway, and the node refused it, because cluster administration over the network requires authentication. The vacuity check described below caught it: a run that promised replica moves had none. The request now runs from inside the target's own network namespace.
  • A clock library that broke sleep. The first clock-skew shim was libfaketime. Under .NET 10 it made timed waits return at once, so the test subject was a database with no timers. The shim is now a small C library that moves the wall clock and leaves monotonic time alone.
  • A client check on one sample. A soak with every database signal clean failed on the load generator's thread-pool queue, which peaked at 103 against a bar of 100 for one second. The rule now judges the queue on dwell time and the 95th percentile. In the same run a fault aimed at the leader was skipped, because one placement sweep taken mid-election saw no leader. The resolver now sweeps every half second for up to ten seconds.
  • An idle disk probe that predicted nothing. We waited up to three hours for the host's idle fsync latency to drop below a threshold before a soak. It read 2.4 to 3.1 ms the whole time on a rebooted idle host, and the run then opened at 0.05 ms anyway. The in-run regime rules are the signal. The gate is gone.

A run whose fault never fired now fails​

A fault that never fires leaves a green run behind. The node-removal item above was found by a rule we added for exactly that reason. A scenario can now declare that it requires a range split, or a replica move, and the harness fails the run as vacuous when the placement samples show neither happened.

That rule guards four new scenarios. Two run key-range sharding, where a table is split into ranges by key and the ranges move between nodes as they grow. The seeded data starts a cascade of splits that outlasts the warm-up, and a partition and a kill land while ranges still split. Two run replica placement on five nodes with three replicas each: a kill at 25 seconds, then a decommission at 80 seconds that drains every replica the node hosts onto the others, so the cluster finishes the run with four nodes. Each pair has an Elle arm, which looks for isolation anomalies in a list-append history, and a bank arm, where the conserved sum and the per-row ledger see a row that a split copy or a seeded replica lost.

Both features are opt-in. The consistency report listed them as the two weakest verified parts of the system. They now have CamusDB-level scenarios that run every night.

Clock skew faults and nightly CI runs​

Part one promised clocks that disagree between nodes. Caraxes can now move one node's wall clock forward or back, by up to twelve hours, and move it back on heal. Only the wall clock moves, so the fault reaches the hybrid logical clock and every lease built on it. Raft elections use monotonic time, so they are unaffected.

Four scenarios target what a given skew can reach: 2 seconds on three nodes as a control, a jump past the 5-second snapshot clock fence, a jump past the 15-second intent and prepare lease, and 3 minutes forward then 1 minute back, past the gossip and schema leases. All four passed with a serializable Elle history. One change came out of them: Kahuna now refuses a snapshot read whose timestamp leads the node's clock, and no longer serves it unfenced.

Caraxes also has CI now. Tests run on every push. Every night at 05:00 UTC a workflow builds CamusDB from main and runs the ten Elle list-append scenarios, one job per scenario. The nightly runs in a correctness-only mode: the recovery-time and throughput rules are reported as not graded, because a hosted runner's speed says nothing about the change. Elle, the ledger, the divergent-apply check, node health and the total-outage rule still grade the run.

Three performance findings​

The harness is also how we measure speed, and three of its findings in this period were about the measurement or the client.

  • TLS has no measurable CPU cost. A pair of ten-minute runs on one image, with the client path in TLS and in cleartext, read 9,082 and 9,240 operations per second at an identical 0.90 CPU-milliseconds per operation on the leader. Cleartext is now the control shape. Raft keeps its certificate.
  • A pipelined client that landed on the wrong node. The new client sends a transfer as two frames instead of six exchanges. Its first measurement was 5,029 operations per second against 9,236 for the sequential client. A pipelined statement carried no routing negotiation, so two thirds of first frames began on a follower, and follower CPU per operation went up four times. With routing fixed in client 0.15.1 the pipelined arm reads 5,737. The second frame, two updates and a commit, costs 27.9 ms against 13.6 ms for the same statements sent one by one. That question is open.
  • A thread pool with a floor of 1,024. Scheduler statistics put 6.8 of the leader's 8.3 cores in 233 to 284 pool workers, at 29 to 33 time slices per client operation, on a host with 16 hardware threads. The server's default minimum of 1,024 threads is what lets the pool grow that far. The pair at a floor of 64 and 128 is the next run.

Behavior of the database today​

  • A node that runs out of memory was a deployment problem. Every Caraxes node runs with MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, the Raft log's index blocks are charged to the shared storage budget, and node memory peaks between 80 and 93 percent of 4 GiB over two hours and comes down between faults.
  • A partition whose voters share a hole in the log elects a leader.
  • A replica that diverges is contained. It gives up leadership, withholds its candidacy, and is re-seeded. A restart that leaves unresolved by-reference records gates at detection, before the node can win a term.
  • A snapshot install cannot skip over a gap, an import cannot rewind below the apply cursor, and a leader does not re-seed a peer that catches up on its own.
  • A vote is judged by term and index on both sides.
  • Log retention is sized in time as well as entries, so a faster commit path does not shrink the window a 30-second restart needs.
  • A re-driven prepare whose first copy settled is rejected, instead of installed as a phantom.

The last pair on a published stack, Kahuna 1.11.7 and Kommander 1.10.7, is double green.

CheckSettle path offSettle path on
Conservationexactexact
Lost rows, divergent applies, unresolved records0, 0, 00, 0, 0
Faults recovered14 of 1413 of 13
Longest recovery0.9 s0.7 s
Snapshot installs00
Pauses repaired by backfill4 of 43 of 3
Memory peak90%90%

The settle-path arm injected thirteen faults. One pause aimed at the leader was skipped by the resolver bug listed above, which is fixed since.

CamusDB today pins a Kahuna three releases past that pair. The pin is ahead of its evidence, as it was in part two, and the next soak closes that gap.

Three more rules for fault testing​

Run long. Some bugs need two hours. Every ten-minute run in part two plateaued at 3.3 to 3.9 GB and passed. In hindsight those plateaus were the memory wall, a few hundred megabytes away. Only a long run with the same budget proves a bound.

Measure the quantity directly. The table-reader ratio of 8.9 percent was right, and the SST volume it was multiplied against was never measured. The inference said 34 GB. The gauge said 262 MB. Two subsystem hypotheses failed in a row for the same reason, and the one that held came from reading the process maps.

Change one thing. The sum came back short by 2 on a pack that changed two things. The control arm with the settle path on, same pack, same schedule, passed, and that isolated the loss to the by-reference replay in one run. Three soaks died of memory, and the fix was one environment variable with no code change.

Part two's third rule held as well. The chain from the first soak to the latest is memory, then a wedge, then a divergence, then a livelock, then an install loop, then two lost writes, then a re-seed storm. Every fix uncovered the next failure when it removed the one in front of it.

The next runs are the kill matrix under load, a second kill window measured on a device that holds its regime, and the two open questions from the performance side.

item.title: What the dragon found: defects from a month of chaos testing
item.description: A dragon breaking one pyramid in a city of glowing pyramids
item.content:encoded:
This post lists the defects that one month of chaos tests found in CamusDB, how we fixed each one, and how the database behaves today. If you are evaluating CamusDB, it shows which failure cases have a test behind them.

Caraxes is our test tool. It runs a real cluster and injects node failures, network faults, and disk faults while a workload runs. This is the second post about it.

Commits and releases in one month​

CamusDB runs on two lower layers. Kahuna is the replicated key-value store under the SQL engine. Kommander is the Raft implementation under Kahuna. A chaos run attacks all three at once, so a finding can land in any of them.

Some terms in this post:

  • Raft: the protocol with which nodes agree on the order of writes. The data is divided into partitions. Each partition has one leader that accepts writes and followers that copy its log.
  • Quorum: a majority of the copies of a partition.
  • Backfill and snapshot: a leader sends missing log entries to a follower that is behind (backfill). If those entries no longer exist, because the log was compacted, it sends a full copy of the state (snapshot).
  • Wedge: a partition or a key that stops making progress and does not recover by itself.
  • Gateway: the node that receives a client request.
  • fsync: the system call that forces a write to the disk.
  • Soak: a long test run.

Between the first post and this one, the three repositories received a large amount of work. Most of it came from a Caraxes run that failed.

RepositoryCommits since 2026-08-19Releases consumed by CamusDB
CamusDB150
Kahunaabout 13345 versions, from 1.0.6 to 1.9.2
Kommanderabout 110from 1.2.x to 1.7.6

Caraxes itself has about 200 scenario files. Many of them carry a long header that reads like a lab notebook. The header records what the previous run showed, what changed for this run, and what result counts as a pass. The rest of this post is a walk through those notebooks.

A lost half of a transfer: the sum fell by three​

The first post explained our strongest check. A workload moves money between random accounts, and the total of all balances must be exactly the same at the end. We call it the bank workload.

The first bank run that failed this check was a two-hour run, with random faults, on an early build. The sum went down by three units.

BeforeAfterDifference
2,993,071,5532,993,071,550-3

Three units out of three billion prove that one transaction applied only half of a transfer. We spent days on this one.

The cause was in the SQL engine. When CamusDB reads a row from Kahuna, the answer can be a confirmed value, a confirmed absence, or a non-answer. A non-answer means the read timed out, or the key was in the middle of replication, or that key returned an error.

The read path treated the non-answer as an absence. From there, the failure was quiet at every step:

  1. The UPDATE for one side of the transfer looked for the row and found nothing.
  2. A match of zero rows is not an error, so the statement reported success.
  3. The transaction committed with one leg of the transfer missing.
  4. Commit validation saw nothing wrong, because the read recorded no observation to validate.

The fix is a contract that now applies to every read path in the engine: a read that cannot confirm the state of a key must fail the statement. It must never report absence. A regression test in the engine carries the run name and the missing three units in its comments.

We also added a tripwire in the workload. If an UPDATE matches zero rows right after a SELECT that found the row, the transfer throws. That way, the same class of bug appears as a failed transfer, which is easier to see than a small drift in a sum.

A partition that stopped while every node reported healthy​

A busy partition changed leader after a fault. The new leader started a backfill for a follower. A heartbeat acknowledgement with no report made the leader believe the follower was at entry one, so the backfill started at entry one. The follower's log was already compacted, so it refused. The refusal never escalated, and the partition stopped committing. Permanently.

During all that time, every node reported ready. The cluster health endpoint said three of three nodes up, healthy, for 83 minutes, while the workload made zero progress.

The fix in Kommander removed the fabricated anchor. Two more releases removed a side effect, where the refusal escalated into a full snapshot on every election. The larger change was in how Caraxes and CamusDB judge health:

  • Caraxes detects a wedge by commit progress, never by node liveness. A window with zero operations during a fault fails the run.
  • CamusDB gained a degraded-partition detector. A partition whose leader has an open backfill refusal, or a snapshot rescue that never converges, is reported as degraded even while its healthy quorum keeps committing.
  • Caraxes now probes every node during the run and grades outages against the fault timeline. A node that dies while its container stays up fails the run. This rule exists because one run passed with a dead node inside a green container.

The same family produced smaller fixes. A snapshot install loop sent 76 installs to one follower in 13 minutes without convergence. A step-down that raced an in-flight proposal left callers with no reply, no failure, and no timeout. A node did not rejoin after a SIGSTOP pause. Each one was found by a run that stalled at a specific minute, with a specific seed, and was fixed against a repeat of that run.

A stale key that took eight runs to fix​

The longest chain in the notebooks started with a 45-minute run named R and ended with a run named Z. Every run in the chain used the same seed, the same faults, and the same workload. Only the engine changed.

RunResultWhat we learned
RSum off by 81, durableA replica that held a write intent deferred its own transaction's materialization forever. Reads then served the older revision.
SSum off by 2The lost units were the first commit at the start of a wedge. The wedged key refused every write until the end of the run.
TSum off by 1, for 46 minutesThe new self-repair read from the wedged node's own state, which was itself behind, so it repaired nothing.
UPass, with two keys wedged read-onlyThe repair's single retry was lost in the same pause that caused the miss. Nothing re-armed it.
VCould not seedThe new armed repair turned a cheap false alarm into a storm: about 1,000 re-drives per node in under a minute.
WPassThe repair now verifies a miss off the actor before it acts.
XFail, same build as W38 rows were frozen up to 186 commits behind in scans, while the aggregates were fully caught up.
Y, ZPass, twiceA durable head that only moves forward. Zero refusal lines across all nodes for the whole window.

Two rules came out of this chain.

The first rule is that one clean window is weak evidence. Run W passed and the identical run X failed. Now a build must pass two consecutive windows before we call it stable.

The second rule is that the aggregate cannot see a stale key. Run U conserved the sum exactly, while one row sat one commit behind on every node. Now the verdict reads the sum in two ways, through the aggregate and through a full row scan, and both must agree.

Scans that dropped rows under write load​

The post-run check counts rows on a quiet cluster. For weeks it passed every time. Then we added a probe that runs SELECT COUNT(*) on every gateway every few seconds during the load.

Under load, the count returned between 1,962 and 1,999 rows out of 2,000. On every gateway. A scan dropped a row that a point read returned. The row was resident, written after the page started, and a non-snapshot page evaluated it as a snapshot read, then dropped it on a miss from the archive.

The second half of the bug was in CamusDB. A read-only scan carried a transaction id, so the MVCC pin in Kahuna could abort a retried page. (MVCC keeps several revisions of a row, so a read sees one point in time.) One arm of a device-pause run produced 365 aborts out of 399 read-only counts. Read-only statements now carry no transaction id.

A related finding was much louder. A pessimistic run with serializable isolation wedged the cluster. Two nodes each read more than 645 GiB from a data directory of 118 MB, and the cluster could not serve one aggregate thirty minutes after the load stopped. A prefix scan with a pinned read timestamp walked the full revision history of every key, and the bank workload leaves each hot row with hundreds of revisions.

The probe is now part of the verdict. A short count is never tolerated, and a run without the probe prints that fact next to its result, because a run that did not test scan visibility proves less than its pass suggests.

Memory growth: one configuration cause and four leaks​

The two-hour runs started to die at minute 88, then at minute 105. Nodes were OOM-killed (stopped by the operating system for lack of memory), or entered a garbage collection spiral with the container up at 110% CPU and the REST port unreachable.

The first cause had no defect in it. The .NET runtime caps its heap at 75% of the container limit by default. The heap plus the native memory of the storage engine added up to more than the container. A node under load long enough to reach its budget died with nothing wrong in the code.

The second cause was ours. Fixed cache floors pinned about 700 MB in caches for a working set of a few megabytes. The floors now yield to a proportional share when the container is small, and every Caraxes node runs with an explicit heap budget of 60% of its limit.

After that, the memory findings became real leaks, and each one has a number.

FindingMeasuredFix
One retained async state machine per gateway request2,906,601 retained objects against 2,912,492 requests on one nodeConstant-memory stream bookkeeping. Live growth fell from 0.258 to 0.039 KiB per operation.
Raft log reclamation could not keep up with ingest277 MB to 1,153 MB in ten minutesThe reclaim floor advances to the true floor on every pass, instead of a fixed number of entries.
Raft log write-ahead files pinned by a column family that never flushed443 MiB to 2,709 MiB in ten minutes, per nodeMetadata column family made flushable, and a cap on total write-ahead size.
Durable transaction records retained by age onlyFilled a 2,458 MiB heap in about five minutes at 8,000 ops/sRetention budget by count and by bytes, plus a heap-pressure valve.

A faster commit path without a memory fix makes a long run worse, because the run reaches the memory knee sooner. In one pair of runs, 5.8 times the throughput bought a decay that started 3.3 times earlier.

The last row of the table hid a second bug. An out-of-memory exception swallowed inside a write-ahead log write left a follower reachable and healthy, with its queue pinned at 4,096 and zero batches for four minutes. The run continued on a reduced quorum. We call this the zombie rule now: a node whose write counter stops while the busiest node keeps writing disqualifies the run, because the test claims to measure a cluster with all its replicas.

Slow disks: a new fault and three engine changes​

The first post listed a full disk as the only disk fault. Long runs showed a second kind: a slow disk.

During long runs on the benchmark host, the NVMe device produced fsync excursions of up to 3.2 seconds under sustained load. An in-flight commit then waited past its 15-second finalize budget and returned an unresolved outcome to the client. Healthy followers logged the stalled leader as unavailable. Nothing crashed, and nothing was wrong with the network.

So Caraxes gained a slow-disk fault. It caps one node's block writes through the kernel's I/O controller, on demand, at a chosen rate. The default rate is a device pause: one 4 KiB write per second. The process, its network, and its peers stay healthy while every durable write waits at the block layer.

That fault drove three changes in the engine:

  • A leader steps down cleanly on its own disk pause, and a follower's disk pause is ridden out from the log.
  • Kahuna rides out a single node's disk pause without unknown outcomes.
  • A local watchdog detects a durable write that stalls, so a node whose disk stopped answering no longer looks healthy.

A related gate compared a build with single-fsync commit on and off, under kills and partitions, with three seeds. The first pass failed the off arm with real data loss: the sum was short by one, and one row was short by five with zero indeterminate attempts, so no ambiguity band could explain it. The on arm passed. We repeated the gate with three more seeds, because one failure and one pass cannot separate a flag that helps from a flag that got lucky. Single-fsync commit is the default today.

The same campaign hardened restarts. A node restarted under load could take a snapshot for a log that already covered the floor, and then livelock on a tombstone. A node that restarted while a peer was briefly unreachable crashed at startup. Both are now regular scenarios.

One node led every partition while requests looked balanced​

A three-node run split its requests almost perfectly across the three gateways, at 33.4%, 33.3%, and 33.4%. The report called it distributed. In the same run, one node led every partition, and one disk did 100% of the durable write work. One node logged about 500,000 key-value entries while the other two logged fewer than 2,000.

The leader balancer was on. It planned six moves and reported five timeouts, and it never emitted a success at all. A transfer suggestion addressed to the node that runs the balancer took an in-process shortcut instead of the transport, and every one of those moves was dropped. The drop paths logged at debug level, so a balancer that failed five of six moves was silent at the default log level.

The transport shortcut is fixed, and a lagging transfer target is now caught up within a bounded wait. Caraxes now waits for leadership to spread before a capacity window opens, and it fails a run that opens with all leaders on one node. An even gateway share says nothing about which disk does the writes.

Six false alarms from the test setup​

Several of the most useful entries in the notebooks are findings against the measurement.

  • A twelve-table seed appeared to stall for six hours and eighteen minutes. Three node logs fell silent in the same second and resumed together. The first reading was a defect report against the database. The laptop had slept. Caraxes now compares a monotonic clock with wall time, and a run whose host slept fails without exception.
  • A dependency bump looked like it cost 38% of throughput. We rebuilt the same commit with one character changed, the dependency version, and the bump cost 6.2%. Four commits in CamusDB owned the rest. A bisect on one merge commit separated two candidates cleanly.
  • Two arms with byte-identical binaries differed by 1.36x, and run order predicted throughput with a correlation of -0.963. Two recorded findings were retracted. Every performance comparison now runs as interleaved pairs in the order base, candidate, candidate, base, and a pair that disagrees in direction is refused.
  • The host NVMe serves the first 30 to 35 GB of a run from a write cache, then changes regime. Where that boundary lands depends on what the previous run left in the cache. Caraxes now writes fsynced ballast during warm-up so every run measures the same regime.
  • A closed-loop run reported 1,182 ops/s with 29.994 requests in flight against a cap of 32. That number was a limit of the load generator. The verdict now records the generator's own CPU and queue depth and can fail a capacity run whose client had no headroom.
  • The container memory figure from Docker counts page cache and kernel memory together with the process. A tool now splits it into cache, native, unused heap, and live data, so a growth curve says which component grew.

Each of these produced a check that now runs on every later run.

Group commit settings that changed defaults​

The write-ahead log on the leader never grouped commits. It wrote exactly one operation per batch at every concurrency from 32 to 256 workers. The group commit linger defaults to zero, and the cluster baseline never set it. So a defect report to the Raft layer would have been wrong.

The measurements that followed changed defaults:

KnobMeasuredDecision
Linger of 1, 3, or 5 msIdentical batches at full occupancyLeft alone. The linger is inert on a single hot partition by design.
Post-completion hold of 2 ms51 to 110 items per round at 128 workers, 6% more throughput, lower write p50Now the default.
Two or four in-flight batches per partition15 to 20% lower throughputDefault stays at one.
Direct reads in the storage engineLeader reads from 1 ms to 40 to 50 ms with the CPU idleShips off.

Behavior of the database today​

  • Unknown is never absent. A read that cannot confirm a key fails the statement. A commit whose transport failed after submission reports an unresolved outcome, and the client retries the same commit on the same handle, instead of a definite-looking error that hides a landed write.
  • A stale leader cannot write. Proposals carry an expected term, quorum checks are on by default, and a leader that lost quorum learns it.
  • A published commit index never runs ahead of durable storage. The checkpoint floor advances only when every entry below it is on disk.
  • A wedge is loud. Backfill refusals, non-converging rescues, and stalled durable writes are reported by the node, and the harness fails a run with zero progress under a fault.
  • Memory has budgets. Retention is bounded by count and bytes, batch streams use constant memory, and storage budgets derive from the real heap limit.
  • The disk can pause and the cluster survives, with no unknown outcomes for a single paused node.
  • Every crash leaves evidence. Crash dumps live outside the data volume, node logs are captured before teardown, and the harness records which build, which durability settings, and which host produced every number.

The scenarios from the first post still run, and their recovery numbers are the ones we compare from build to build.

ScenarioFaultPeak error rateRecovery after heal
Kill a node during transfersSIGKILL for 20 seconds100%5.5 s
Kill a whole zoneTwo nodes of six, 30 seconds100%4.1 s
Full diskData volume filled to the last byte, 15 seconds25%1.6 s

In the full disk case, the node refused writes with a clean error, kept serving reads, and accepted writes again with no restart as soon as space came back.

Kommander also gained an in-process simulation with seeded faults, trace shrinking, and invariant checkers, and Kahuna can now start a multi-node cluster in one process with link blocks and restarts. Caraxes found the failures at the level of a real cluster in Docker. These simulators reproduce them in milliseconds inside a unit test, so a fix comes with a test that fails on the old code.

Three rules for fault testing​

Check invariants first. Every serious correctness bug in this post was found by a number that did not add up, and only then explained by a log. Engine-side analysis of the logs alone ran out of evidence more than once. A per-row ledger of every transfer, joined against the seeded baseline, is what turned a deficit we could count into a deficit we could attribute.

Test the measurement too. A sleeping laptop, a busy host, a write cache, and a saturated load generator all produced findings that looked exactly like database defects. Each one now has a check that runs on every run.

Expect each fix to reveal the next bug. The chain from run R to run Z is eight fixes deep, and every fix uncovered the next failure by removing the one in front of it.

Some scenarios in the notebooks still have open questions, and a few new faults are on the list.

item.title: Game wallets and inventories need distributed transactions
item.description: Why we treat every player inventory and wallet as a small bank account, and why that leads a game backend to distributed transactions.
item.content:encoded:
This post explains why a game backend needs distributed transactions for player wallets and inventories. You will see the argument against them, three reasons it fails for a game economy, and what a safe trade looks like in SQL. If you design a game backend, the post ends with five requirements for the database that holds player value.

A player spends forty hours to earn a sword. Another player pays real money for a bundle of skins. A guild saves gold for three weeks to buy a fortress. To the player, that is time, money, and trust. When a backend loses an item or duplicates a currency, the player reads it as disrespect.

We run game backends on CamusDB today, and we treat every inventory and every wallet as a small bank account.

A game economy is a ledger​

  • A wallet is an account with a balance that must never go below zero.
  • An inventory is a set of assets, and each asset has exactly one owner.
  • A shop purchase is a transfer: currency leaves one account, an item enters another.
  • A trade between two players is a transfer in both directions, at the same instant.
  • A guild bank is a shared account with many writers.
  • A season reward is a credit that must be granted exactly once.

These are the rules a bank enforces. The amounts are smaller, and the number of accounts is often larger.

balance >= 0
one item -> one owner
one reward -> granted once
a trade completes for both sides, or for neither

A game backend must enforce each rule on every operation, as a bank does, because one broken rule costs the trust of the player.

The single-threaded shard argument​

There is a popular argument in the game backend world. It deserves a fair statement before we answer it.

A shard is one slice of the game data, for example one region of the world, that lives on one machine. The argument goes like this:

  • A transaction that touches data on several machines needs network round trips.
  • A transaction that waits on a network round trip holds its locks for a millisecond. A local transaction holds them for a few microseconds.
  • If two transactions touch the same busy row (a hot row), the second one waits for the first.
  • A single thread on a single machine can process a hot row hundreds of thousands of times per second. A distributed commit on that same row processes it about a thousand times per second.

Therefore, the argument says, keep each region of the game world in one single-threaded shard. Keep the transactions local. Pass messages between shards asynchronously. Reserve distributed transactions for rare cases, or avoid them completely.

The physics in that argument is correct. A network round trip is slower than a memory access, and ten machines cannot update one row faster than one machine can.

The conclusion fails for games, for three reasons.

Reason one: the valuable transactions cross the shard boundary​

The argument assumes that transactions across shards are rare and unimportant. In a game economy, they carry the value:

  • A trade between two players who met in different regions.
  • A deposit into a guild bank from a member who plays on another continent.
  • A marketplace sale, where the seller and the buyer are never in the same place.
  • A gift from one account to another.
  • A player who walks from one region to another with a full inventory.
  • A cross-server event that pays a reward to every participant.

These are less frequent than movement updates. They also have the most real money, the most player hours, and the most exploit attempts behind them.

A shard model that makes local work fast and cross-shard work unsafe leaves the most valuable transactions to hand-written code.

Reason two: asynchronous messages between shards cause duplicates​

If two shards cannot commit together, a trade between them becomes a conversation. Shard A removes the sword and sends a message. Shard B receives the message and adds the sword.

  • If B is down, A must remember to retry.
  • If A crashes after the removal and before the send, the sword is gone.
  • If the message is delivered twice, the sword exists twice.
  • If a player logs out during the hand-off between regions, the inventory can exist on both regions, or on neither.

Item duplication exploits have this shape. The usual fix has three parts:

  • Idempotency keys: a unique key per operation, so a repeat has no effect.
  • Outbox tables: a table of messages that are saved with the change and sent later.
  • Compensation steps: code that undoes the first half when the second half fails.

A reconciliation job then runs at night and files the differences into a spreadsheet. Together, that is a distributed transaction protocol, often called a saga. The game team writes it under a release deadline, and writes it again for each new feature that crosses a boundary.

A database with distributed transactions does that work once, in one place, and tests it against node failures. The cost is a millisecond at commit.

Reason three: the hot key belongs to the simulation​

The strongest part of the argument is the hot row. A world boss with one health value takes hits from two hundred players at once. A single-threaded engine can process that. A distributed commit cannot, at that rate.

The ledger does not need that rate. Games already separate two kinds of state:

  • Simulation state lives in the game server, in memory, and changes on every tick (one step of the game loop). Position, health, cooldowns, projectiles. It is rebuilt from scratch when a match starts, and it is allowed to lose a few ticks when a server dies.
  • Ledger state lives in the database. Wallets, inventories, ownership, purchase history, progression. It is never rebuilt from scratch, and it is never allowed to lose one entry.

The boss fight is simulation. The loot at the end of the fight is ledger, and the ledger sees one transaction per player at the end.

What remains for the database is a ledger workload: many accounts, low contention per account, and a strict need for atomicity when two accounts change together. A distributed SQL database is built for that workload.

Coordination cost applies only to transactions that cross partitions​

A fair objection remains. If every commit pays for a distributed protocol, the ledger becomes slow for the common case too.

CamusDB splits the key space into partitions. Each partition has one leader node and a log that is replicated to the other nodes with Raft, a consensus protocol. A table and its secondary indexes live under one key prefix, and that prefix maps to one partition by default.

A transaction that touches one partition commits through that one leader. Two-phase commit, the protocol that makes several partitions commit together, runs only when a transaction writes to more than one partition.

  • A shop purchase that changes one wallet and one inventory usually commits on one leader, with one replicated log round.
  • A trade between two players whose rows live on different partitions pays for two-phase commit.
  • A read-only report over the whole economy runs from one consistent snapshot, without a lock, and without a block on writers.

When a table becomes hot, key-range sharding can split it into ranges and place those ranges on different leaders. The split moves data placement. A transaction that spans two ranges is still one transaction. See Key-range sharding and Distributed transactions and HLC for the details.

Example: a trade between two players​

Player 10 gives a sword and receives 500 gold. Player 20 gives 500 gold and receives the sword.

The wallet table carries the bank rule as a constraint, so the database enforces it on every update:

CREATE TABLE wallets (
  player_id INT64 NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  balance INT64 NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

The trade is one transaction. It has an idempotency key, so a client retry cannot execute it twice.

BEGIN;

UPDATE wallets
SET balance = balance - 500
WHERE player_id = 20;

UPDATE wallets
SET balance = balance + 500
WHERE player_id = 10;

UPDATE items
SET owner_id = 20
WHERE item_id = 88123 AND owner_id = 10;

INSERT INTO trades (trade_key, seller_id, buyer_id, item_id, price)
VALUES ('7f3a9c1e-trade-2026-09-07', 10, 20, 88123, 500);

COMMIT;

Four things protect the players here:

  • If player 20 cannot pay, the first update violates the check constraint. The statement fails, and the transaction commits nothing.
  • If player 10 no longer owns the sword, the third update changes zero rows. The application sees that count and rolls back.
  • The unique index on trade_key rejects a second attempt with the same key.
  • Serializable isolation is the default: the result is the same as if the transactions ran one at a time. A concurrent trade of the same sword to a third player conflicts, and one of the two transactions retries. The application replays the loser from BEGIN.

The two wallets and the item can live on three different partitions. The transaction still commits on all of them or on none of them.

A confirmed commit survives a node failure​

If CamusDB confirms a commit, that commit survives, even if the node that confirmed it dies one second later.

  • A committed write goes through the replicated partition log before the client hears "ok".
  • A leader change continues from a log state that Raft made safe.
  • A transaction that did not reach a durable decision is reported as a retry, and the application replays it.

We test that rule with real failures. Our chaos tool, Caraxes, runs money transfers between random accounts while it kills nodes, cuts the network, and fills disks. At the end, the total of all balances must be exactly the same as before. We wrote about that tool in Caraxes: how we test CamusDB against real failures.

An in-memory engine that acknowledges a commit before the write is safe on a second machine benchmarks faster. It also leaves a window in which a player's purchase exists only in the memory of one process, and an item lost in that window was already paid for.

The cost: milliseconds at commit​

A distributed commit in CamusDB costs milliseconds. A local commit costs less. A single-threaded in-memory engine costs microseconds.

A player clicks "accept trade". The round trip from the client to the server is tens of milliseconds, and the animation is half a second. The player cannot perceive the difference between three microseconds and three milliseconds at commit.

The engineering trade is a millisecond at commit against a saga per feature and a reconciliation job at night. Keep the simulation in the tick loop, and keep the ledger in database transactions.

Five requirements for a game database​

We hold CamusDB to this list, and we suggest it for any database that holds player value:

  1. Serializable isolation by default, so a race is a retry and never a duplicate.
  2. Atomic commits across machines, so a trade, a guild deposit, or a region hand-off is one unit of work.
  3. Coordination cost that follows the data, so a local purchase does not pay for a distributed protocol it does not need.
  4. Durability before acknowledgement, so a confirmed purchase survives the death of the node that confirmed it.
  5. Failure tests with an invariant check, so the guarantee is measured on every build.

item.title: Caraxes: how we test CamusDB against real failures
item.description: A dragon burning a city of glowing pyramids at night
item.content:encoded:
This post shows how we test CamusDB against real failures: killed servers, broken networks, and full disks. You will see what the test tool checks, how a test is written, and which failures it covers today. Use it to judge how much evidence stands behind the CamusDB cluster guarantees.

When every server is healthy, almost any database looks correct. The hard cases are a server that dies in the middle of a commit, a network that loses packets, and a disk that fills up during a write. Those cases are hard to create by hand, so we built a tool that creates them on demand. We named it Caraxes, after a dragon, because its job is to attack our own cluster.

A cluster can fail in part​

A database on one server has a simple failure story. The process runs or it does not. When it stops, recovery means one thing: read the write-ahead log (the file that records each change before it is applied) and continue.

A cluster is a group of servers, called nodes, that hold copies of the same data. In a cluster, one node can break while the others keep working, and the others often cannot tell what kind of break they see.

Imagine three nodes, and one of them goes quiet. From outside, these cases look the same:

  • The node crashed.
  • The node is alive but frozen for a few seconds.
  • The node is fine, but the network between it and the others drops packets.

Each case needs a different reaction. A crashed node must be replaced. A frozen node wakes up by itself. A node behind a broken network can still think it is the leader (the node that accepts writes) and can still accept work.

The cluster has to choose a reaction quickly, with missing information.

Silent wrong answers are the dangerous failure​

A wrong answer does more harm than an error, because nobody looks for a problem they were never told about. During a failure, these are the risks:

  • A write is confirmed, then lost when a new leader takes over.
  • A deleted row comes back after an old copy of the data is promoted.
  • A transfer takes money from one account and never adds it to the other.

A normal test suite runs on one healthy machine, with plenty of disk and a perfect network. Those tests are still worth having, but they cannot find any of these problems.

Five properties that Caraxes measures​

Reliability is several properties, and each one needs its own proof.

  • Durability. If we confirm your commit, it survives, even if the node that confirmed it dies one second later.
  • Consistency. You never see half of a transaction, no matter which node answers your query.
  • Availability. The cluster keeps serving while part of it is down.
  • Recovery. After the problem is fixed, the cluster goes back to normal by itself, and fast.
  • Predictability. The same failure behaves the same way every time.

A database can pass four of these and fail the fifth. A cluster that stays correct but needs two minutes to answer queries after it loses one node is still painful to run. Caraxes measures all five in a single run.

A test is one YAML file​

The file says which cluster to build, what load to run, what to break, and what result we expect.

name: kill-follower
cluster:
  name: chaos-kill
  nodes: 3
  partitions: 3
  replication_factor: 3
workload:
  database: caraxes
  rows: 20000
  mode: open
  target_ops: 300
  workers: 32
  duration: 60s
  warmup: 15s
nemesis:
  seed: 7
  events:
    - { at: 20s, fault: kill, target: random, duration: 20s }
checks:
  max_recovery_seconds: 45

One command does the rest. It builds the CamusDB image from the code on your disk, starts a real cluster in Docker, waits until every node is ready, loads a dataset, and sends real SQL traffic through the normal client. Twenty seconds in, it kills a node. Twenty seconds later, it brings the node back.

The failures are real:

  • A kill is a SIGKILL signal, which stops the process at once.
  • A network partition is a firewall rule that drops packets between nodes.
  • A slow link is added latency on the network interface.
  • A full disk is a file that grows until the disk has no space left.

We avoid simulations here, because a simulation only tests the behavior we already imagined.

The run ends with a pass or a fail, so a machine can read the result.

The balance check: total money stays the same​

One of our test workloads moves money between random accounts. Every transfer takes an amount from one row and adds it to another, inside one transaction.

Money only moves, so the total of all balances must be exactly the same after the test as before it. If the total changed, a transaction was not atomic, and the test fails. We apply this check in every test, including the tests that kill a node.

These transfers also make transactions conflict on the same rows. Our other workload avoids conflicts so it can measure speed and failover cleanly, but a test without conflicts cannot catch a broken transaction.

Errors are judged by what the test injected​

If we injected no failure, an internal error is a real bug and the test fails.

If we just killed a node, connections close while requests are still travelling, so a few client-side errors are normal. We count them and print them, but they alone do not fail a test that stayed correct and recovered in time. This keeps the test from failing on every run, which would teach us to ignore it.

Recovery time for every fault​

Caraxes records every break and every repair with exact timestamps. The workload records each second: how many operations succeeded, how many failed, and how slow they were.

Afterwards, we put both records on the same clock. That answers three questions for every failure:

  • How bad did it get?
  • Did the cluster keep doing useful work, or did it stop completely?
  • How many seconds after the repair did things go back to normal?
# Fault analysis

- Normal seconds: error rate 0.00 %, write p99 1,382.0 ms
- During the failure: error rate 40.45 %, write p99 392.9 ms
- Longest recovery: 5.5 s; everything recovered: yes

| fault | healed | window (s) | peak error | failed | progressed | recovery (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| kill/camus2 | yes | 20.3 | 100 % | 4,074 | yes | 5.5 |

In this run we killed a node and errors jumped, but the cluster never stopped completely. 5.5 seconds after the node came back, everything was normal again. We compare that last number from one build to the next. (p99 is the latency that 99% of operations stayed under.)

A seed makes every run repeatable​

Every random choice comes from a seed number. The same seed kills the same node at the same second, in the same order.

When a run fails, we run it again and watch it fail in the same way. After we fix the cause, we run it once more and watch it pass.

Failures covered today​

Each test asks one question.

  • A run with no failures at all, so we know the cluster and the traffic work before we break anything.
  • A node killed in the middle of the run, then restarted.
  • A node cut off from all the others, and separately a node slowed down, so nothing dies but the network stops cooperating.
  • Money transfers running while a node is killed, with the total checked afterwards.
  • Six nodes in three zones, with one entire zone killed, so every partition loses a copy at the same moment and has to survive with two.
  • A node with a full disk, to confirm that it refuses writes without a crash, and accepts them again once there is space.
  • A long run with random failures arriving every ten to eighteen seconds.
  • A test for the leader balancer alone: kill the busiest node, restart it, and check that leadership comes back to it.

A test grid catches regressions​

Recovery time gets worse in small steps. Someone adds a cache, changes a timeout, or moves two lines in the commit path, and a fifteen second recovery becomes fifty. Each change looks fine in review, and all the unit tests still pass, because none of them ever unplugged a server.

So we run a whole grid of tests at once. One file expands into many runs across locking modes, cluster sizes, and failure types. It produces a table with every result and every recovery time side by side. When a change costs us reliability, it shows up as a row that used to pass and now fails.

The result is a pass or fail code that our CI (the automated build and test system) can read.

Planned tests​

  • Deeper correctness checking, to catch strange orderings that a simple total cannot detect.
  • Disks that are slow or that return damaged data.
  • Clocks that disagree between nodes, because time is one of the things a cluster trusts the most.
  • Nodes joining and leaving while traffic is running.
  • Schema changes during failures, since a migration is the worst possible moment to lose a node.
  • Distributed queries during failures, so a query split across the cluster still returns the same rows when one part disappears.
  • Backups and restores while the cluster is under attack.
  • Bigger clusters and much longer runs, because some bugs only appear after hours.

Chaos testing covers only the injected failures​

For each failure that Caraxes injects, a passing run shows that the cluster kept the data correct and recovered in a time we measured and accept. Chaos testing cannot prove that the database has no other bugs.

item.title: A database branch for every AI agent experiment
item.description: AI agents explore several solutions in parallel, and each one needs a realistic database. Copy-on-write branches give every experiment an isolated database that is fast to create and drop.
item.content:encoded:
This post explains how database branches give each experiment an isolated database that is fast to create and to drop. You will see the SQL, how copy-on-write keeps a branch cheap, and the limits of the feature today. It is useful if AI agents or automated jobs test changes against your data.

A developer usually tests one idea at a time. An AI agent can explore several solutions in parallel: one tries a schema migration, another rewrites some data, a third reproduces a bug. Each one needs a realistic database, and none of them must damage the shared starting point.

Parallel experiments interfere on a shared database​

Consider an agent that must improve the checkout flow of an online store. It compares three approaches:

  • Add a new status to the current table.
  • Move payment details into a separate table.
  • Keep the schema and change only the application logic.

If all three use the same database, they interfere. A migration from the first attempt can break the second. Test data from the second can change the result of the third. When something fails, it is hard to tell which action caused it.

The usual response is to create separate databases or to restore the same backup several times. That adds time and operational work, and the cost grows when software creates the experiments.

Create a branch with SQL​

CamusDB creates an isolated branch from a point in time with one statement:

CREATE DATABASE checkout_attempt BRANCH FROM prod;

The new database begins with the schema and data of prod at that moment, the fork point. After that, changes in the branch stay in the branch:

  • New rows do not appear in the parent database.
  • Updates do not replace the parent's values.
  • Deletes do not remove the parent's rows.
  • Schema changes do not alter the parent's structure.

CamusDB does not copy the source rows when it creates the branch. Reads of inherited data use the source snapshot. New writes and schema changes go into a private overlay that the branch owns. This model is called copy-on-write.

So a branch can begin from a large, realistic database with no full copy. Storage grows as the branch diverges from its parent.

Two experiments can start from the same database:

CREATE DATABASE checkout_schema_test BRANCH FROM prod;
CREATE DATABASE checkout_data_repair BRANCH FROM prod;

The first branch tests a migration:

USE checkout_schema_test;

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN payment_reference STRING;
CREATE INDEX orders_payment_reference_idx
ON orders (payment_reference);

The second tests a data change:

USE checkout_data_repair;

UPDATE orders
SET status = "review"
WHERE status = "payment_unknown";

Neither experiment changes prod, and neither branch can see the other branch's work.

Fast creation makes a branch per task practical​

If an isolated environment takes several minutes to create, an agent creates fewer of them. It reuses an old test database, does fewer experiments, or puts several tasks in the same environment. Each of those choices reduces isolation.

When a branch is fast to create, a system can create one for every task, attempt, or test run. Failed branches can be inspected and then removed.

Creation time also affects parallel work. If one task explores eight possible changes, the eight workers can start from the same state at once and move independently.

The agent workflow: branch, change, check, drop​

Many agent workflows follow this pattern:

  1. Start from a known state.
  2. Create one or more isolated branches.
  3. Make a different change in each branch.
  4. Run checks and compare the results.
  5. Keep the useful information and drop the branches.

For example, an agent investigates a bug that appears only in production. It creates several branches from the same point in time. In one branch, it changes an order's status. In another, it removes a related payment record. In a third, it applies a proposed schema fix. Every branch has the same starting point, so the results are easy to compare.

Branches are also useful for these tasks:

  • Rehearse migrations against realistic data.
  • Test data repair scripts before approval.
  • Compare alternative indexing strategies.
  • Generate test cases that modify the database.
  • Run destructive checks in disposable environments.

Each result has a known starting state​

When several workers share one database, a successful test can depend on data that another worker created. A failed test can come from an unrelated migration. A retry can give a different answer, because the starting state changed.

With branches, each attempt has a clear parent and a clear fork point. If an attempt fails, the branch stays available. A developer can query it, examine its schema, and see the exact state that produced the failure.

SHOW BRANCHES and SHOW ANCESTORS show these relationships:

SHOW BRANCHES FROM prod;
SHOW ANCESTORS FROM checkout_schema_test;

They answer three questions: which experiments still exist, where a branch came from, and how deep its history is.

Costs and limits of branches​

A live branch keeps its source snapshot available, so CamusDB cannot always reclaim old history while the branch depends on it. Deep chains of branches also make reads slower, because the database checks several ancestors.

For automated workflows, keep branches focused and short-lived:

  • Create a branch for a specific task.
  • Record the result and any useful diagnostics.
  • Keep failed branches only when they need investigation.
  • Drop branches when the task is complete.
  • Avoid long chains when several branches can start from the same parent.

CamusDB has two limits today:

  • Changes cannot be merged back into the parent.
  • Transactions cannot cross branches.

A successful experiment must produce a reviewed migration, script, or application change, which you apply through the normal delivery process.

item.title: Teaching CamusDB to choose better query plans
item.description: How the CamusDB query optimizer uses dynamic programming and table statistics to choose a join order, and why the search space grows so fast.
item.content:encoded:
This post explains how CamusDB chooses the order in which it joins tables, and why that choice has a large effect on query time. You will see how the search works, how table statistics improve it, and how to enable it and inspect its result with EXPLAIN.

The query optimizer is the part of a database that decides how to run a SQL query. A query can use a table scan, an index lookup, an index range scan, a hash join, a merge join, a nested loop join, a sort, an aggregate, a derived table, or a subquery. Every option gives a correct result, but only some are fast. The optimizer chooses a plan before the query runs.

SQL is declarative. This query says which result the user wants, and gives no order in which to read the tables:

SELECT u.email, p.title, c.body
FROM users u
JOIN posts p ON p.user_id = u.id
JOIN comments c ON c.post_id = p.id
WHERE u.active = true;

The database decides the order.

Join order decides how much data a query reads​

Assume these three tables:

  • users has many rows, but only a few are active.
  • posts has many rows for each user.
  • comments has many rows for each post.

If CamusDB starts with all comments, then joins posts, then joins users, it reads a lot of data before it finds that most rows do not match u.active = true.

If it starts with the active users, it reduces the data much earlier. The result is the same, but the amount of work is very different. So the optimizer has to estimate the cost of each order.

The number of join orders grows fast​

With two tables, there are only a few orders. With five, six, or seven tables, the number of possible orders grows very quickly.

An optimizer could try every order, estimate the cost of each one, and pick the cheapest. That works for tiny cases, but then the optimizer itself becomes too slow.

CamusDB uses dynamic programming for eligible inner joins when cost-based join ordering is enabled. Dynamic programming solves a large problem from the saved answers to smaller ones. This approach comes from System R, an early relational database.

The optimizer asks smaller questions first:

  • What is the best plan for users?
  • What is the best plan for posts?
  • What is the best plan for comments?
  • What is the best plan for users JOIN posts?
  • What is the best plan for posts JOIN comments?

It remembers the best answer for each small set of tables and reuses it to build the answer for a larger set.

The optimizer fills a table of partial plans​

First, the optimizer estimates the best way to read each table. One table can use an index, and another a full scan.

Then it looks at pairs of tables that can be joined. For each pair, it asks:

  • Can this pair be joined with an indexed nested loop?
  • Is a hash join cheaper?
  • Can both sides arrive ordered, so that a merge join is possible?
  • How many rows will probably come out?
  • How expensive is the intermediate result?

Then it does the same for groups of three tables, then four, and so on. Each step builds on the best smaller plans it already found. At the end, it has a plan for the full query.

These are estimates. The optimizer does not know the exact row counts.

The memo table and the recurrence​

The optimizer keeps a memo table:

dp[set of tables] = cheapest known left-deep plan for exactly that set

"Left-deep" is explained in the next section. For a query with three tables, the optimizer first creates entries for single tables:

dp[{users}]
dp[{posts}]
dp[{comments}]

Each entry stores a partial plan, its estimated cost, and the estimated number of rows that it produces.

Then CamusDB builds larger entries from smaller ones:

dp[{users, posts}]
dp[{posts, comments}]
dp[{users, comments}]
dp[{users, posts, comments}]

The recurrence is roughly:

best(S) =
  min over each table R in S:
    best(S - R) joined with R

CamusDB only considers a join when a predicate connects the existing left side and the new right table. That prevents a cross product, which is a join of every row against every row.

For each possible extension, the optimizer asks which join algorithm is cheaper:

  • If the right table has an index on the join key, an indexed nested-loop join can be cheap.
  • If repeated index probes look expensive, a hash join can be cheaper.
  • If both sides can arrive ordered by the join key, a merge join can be a good option.

In simplified form:

candidate_cost =
  cost(best_left_plan)
  + cost(join best_left_plan with next_table)

If the new candidate is cheaper than the current dp[S], it replaces it.

The real implementation has more details, but this is the core.

The search covers left-deep plans only​

A left-deep plan looks like this:

(((users JOIN posts) JOIN comments) JOIN reactions)

The left side grows one table at a time, and each step adds one new table on the right.

In a bushy plan, both sides of a join can be joined subtrees:

(users JOIN posts) JOIN (comments JOIN reactions)

Bushy plans can be useful, but they make the search space larger. For now, CamusDB searches left-deep plans only.

The search has more boundaries:

  • It is used for eligible inner joins.
  • It works with JOIN ... ON predicates that can be safely reordered.
  • It is capped for very wide joins, so planning time stays bounded.
  • Unsupported shapes fall back to the heuristic join order.

Statistics from ANALYZE improve the estimates​

CamusDB can use table statistics, index counts, histograms, min/max values, and distinct-value counts that ANALYZE collects. These values answer questions like:

  • How many rows are in this table?
  • What fraction of the rows does this filter keep?
  • Is this index likely to return a small number of rows?
  • How many rows can this join produce?
ANALYZE TABLE users;
ANALYZE TABLE posts;
ANALYZE TABLE comments;

You can inspect the result with EXPLAIN:

EXPLAIN
SELECT u.email, p.title, c.body
FROM users u
JOIN posts p ON p.user_id = u.id
JOIN comments c ON c.post_id = p.id
WHERE u.active = true;

EXPLAIN shows the selected physical plan with its estimated rows and cost. You can see whether CamusDB picked a hash join, a merge join, an indexed nested loop join, or a fallback nested loop join.

Constraints on the optimizer​

In the real engine, the optimizer has these constraints:

  • It must preserve SQL semantics.
  • It must respect join predicates.
  • It must not reorder joins when that changes the result.
  • It must know which indexes are available.
  • It must estimate row counts from imperfect statistics.
  • It must choose between different join algorithms.
  • It must still produce a plan quickly.

Your part is small: write SQL, create useful indexes, and run ANALYZE when the data changes.

The cost-based optimizer is opt-in​

CamusDB keeps the cost-based optimizer behind configuration flags:

cost_based_access_path_enabled: true
cost_based_join_order_enabled: true

The rule-based planner remains stable and predictable. Enable the cost-based planner when you want CamusDB to compare more plans and use statistics.

item.title: The origins of CamusDB: Spanner, game backends, and .NET
item.description: Why CamusDB exists: years of distributed SQL in game backends, why it is built in .NET, the storage and consensus layers under it, and features such as database branching.
item.content:encoded:
Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.

— Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

This post explains why CamusDB exists, why it is written in .NET, and which projects it is built on. Read it to understand the goals of the database before you evaluate it.

For many years I worked with Google Spanner, and I fell in love with distributed SQL databases. A distributed SQL database stores its data on several servers and keeps transactions consistent across them.

In the video game industry, the database is a critical part of the player experience. Games need to handle spikes, global traffic, competitive systems, economies, inventories, matchmaking, leaderboards, live events, and rewards. All of it must work correctly when thousands or millions of players are active.

Spanner showed me that a database could give strong consistency and scalability at the infrastructure level. Without that, every backend team adds its own workarounds: queues, caches, compensating jobs, and manual repair scripts.

So I asked myself what it would take to build something like this. I wanted to understand the tradeoffs, the hard parts, and the places where I could experiment with ideas that I think are useful.

I began to work on CamusDB in 2021. At the beginning, it felt like a big experiment. A distributed SQL database touches almost every hard problem in backend infrastructure, and that is what makes it exciting to me.

The reasons for .NET​

One question I get often is why I build a database in .NET.

.NET has improved year after year, especially in performance: the JIT compiler, the garbage collector, networking, memory APIs, async code, Native AOT, and the standard libraries. Modern .NET is fast, mature, and capable of serious backend infrastructure workloads.

I have worked with .NET for many years, and I know the ecosystem well. That lets me move fast and keep the system clean and understandable.

For infrastructure projects, .NET has earned its place next to Go, Rust, C++, and Java.

The layers under CamusDB: Kahuna and Kommander​

For years I built the lower-level infrastructure that CamusDB needs.

  • Kahuna is a distributed key/value and locking layer. It provides the coordination and the transactional primitives that CamusDB uses as its foundation.
  • Kommander is the Raft library under Kahuna. Raft is a protocol with which servers agree on the order of writes. It looks simple in the paper, but an implementation that survives failure tests has many details.

CamusDB sits on top of that work: distributed coordination, locks, key/value storage, replication, consensus, and transactions.

Freedom to add features such as database branching​

When you work on your own database, you can add features that you believe are useful, even if mainstream systems do not have them yet.

One example is database branching. A branch is an isolated copy of your data for tests, development, experiments, previews, or risky changes. You create it without a manual clone of everything and without a set of fragile environments.

The feature comes from real pain. In backend and game development, we constantly need safe environments to validate economy changes, content updates, migrations, live event configurations, and backend behavior, with no effect on production data.

The scope of a distributed SQL database​

A distributed SQL database includes query planning, transactions, distributed execution, indexes, consistency, replication, schema changes, locking, fault tolerance, storage, and snapshots. Each of these can break in subtle ways.

Every feature forces me to understand the system more deeply, and every design decision has a tradeoff.

Current state​

CamusDB is becoming a real database with real capabilities, on top of infrastructure that took years to design and implement. There is still a lot to do. The goal is to make strong consistency and scalability more accessible.
